explanation: B is correct because batch ModelMonitor directly handles feature drift with baselines, schedules jobs, and integrates with CloudWatch/SNS. A and D are custom and more maintenance. C misuses Clarify drift detector instead of ModelMonitor.

stem: A retail company uses multi-model endpoints. They must monitor data skew separately for each model under high invocation volume without overloading S3. How should they configure Model Monitor?

answers.A: Enable DataCaptureConfig for all models to a single S3 prefix and schedule a single monitor job with a filter script per model.
answers.B: Use one monitor schedule per model, each writing to its own S3 bucket to avoid prefix collision.
answers.C: Configure DataCaptureConfig to drop 80% of captured requests, tag model name, and run a single monitor job with group-by on model name.
answers.D: Disable DataCaptureConfig, and use CloudWatch synthetic tests per model for skew detection.

explanation: C is correct: sampling reduces S3 volume, tagging allows a single job with group-by to monitor each model. A writes all data and requires filtering inside job. B duplicates resources. D uses synthetic tests, not real capture.

stem: An AI startup uses Clarify ModelExplainabilityMonitor for drift detection, but they notice that on Mondays, due to different user behavior, alerts spike falsely. They want to suppress Monday alerts but keep daily checks. Which modification is appropriate?

answers.A: Add a suppression rule in CloudWatch alarm for Mondays using a schedule-based mute period.
answers.B: Adjust the drift threshold upward only for Monday’s monitoring schedule.
answers.C: Exclude data collected on Mondays from the ModelExplainabilityMonitor input baseline.
answers.D: Shift monitoring schedule to every 48 hours to skip Monday checks.

explanation: A is correct: CloudWatch alarm suppression allows muting alerts on Mondays without affecting thresholds. B leads to inconsistent drift sensitivity. C corrupts baseline. D reduces monitoring frequency overall.

stem: A ride-sharing company deployed a streaming inference endpoint. They need to detect concept drift in the predicted probability distribution for rider surge events. Which built-in capability supports this?

answers.A: ModelQualityMonitor’s custom metrics for probability shift detection.
answers.B: ModelMonitor’s ModelBiasMonitor class with a custom preprocessor to compute Jensen-Shannon divergence.
answers.C: ModelExplainabilityMonitor with SHAP-based drift metrics.
answers.D: DefaultModelMonitor data quality checks for distribution changes.

explanation: B is correct because ModelBiasMonitor can measure probability distribution drift of predictions using divergence metrics. A is not a ModelQualityMonitor feature. C focuses on feature importance. D checks data quality, not prediction distribution.

stem: A gaming company wants to use SageMaker Model Monitor to detect anomalies in user behavior predictions every five minutes but must avoid executing on cold data. The endpoint has periods of very low traffic. How to configure?

answers.A: Schedule monitoring at 5-minute intervals without sampling; it will skip if no new data.
answers.B: Use 1-minute schedule with a Lambda filter to drop empty datasets.
answers.C: Configure ModelMonitor with max_runtime per job to 10 minutes so it exits on no data.
answers.D: Schedule monitoring every 5 minutes with min_sampling_size set to 50 so it won’t run unless at least 50 records are present.

explanation: D is correct: min_sampling_size prevents jobs when insufficient data arrives, avoiding waste. A will run and error on empty data. B and C require custom code or rely on runtime but don’t prevent job attempts.

stem: An energy company’s endpoint serves predictions at different times of day, with nightly off-peak periods. They need to monitor inference anomalies only during peak hours (8 AM–8 PM). Which pattern accomplishes this?

answers.A: Create a monitor schedule at 1-hour intervals and ignore anomalies logged outside of 8–20 via filter in the alerting Lambda.
answers.B: Use two monitoring schedules: one at 5-minute intervals active between 8 and 20 using schedule expressions, and none outside that window.
answers.C: Enable continuous monitoring and write a custom script to drop anomalies outside the window.
answers.D: Schedule a daily monitor job at 20:01 that covers the day’s peak data.

explanation: B is correct: schedule expressions in SageMaker allow cron-based windows to run only during peak hours. A adds complexity. C and D don’t align to real-time peak detection.

stem: A financial app uses a multi-variant endpoint to serve A/B test models. They need to compare real-time inference accuracy of each variant for rollout decisions without manual intervention. Which integrated feature achieves this?

answers.A: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query variant-specific logs and compute accuracy per variant.
answers.B: Enable Kinesis Data Streams on endpoint traffic, write a consumer to compute variant accuracy.
answers.C: Use SageMaker Model Monitor’s built-in endpoint variant-based shadow testing with baseline accuracy thresholds and CloudWatch alarms.
answers.D: Invoke two separate endpoints in parallel and use Lambda to compare results against ground truth.

explanation: C is correct: Model Monitor supports shadow variants for model comparison against baselines, automating monitoring. A and B require manual aggregation. D duplicates endpoints and custom code.

stem: A telecom provider must ensure that no single categorical feature ‘device_type’ in production grows in usage by more than 20% relative to training. They want to monitor this continuously. Which approach is best?

answers.A: Use ModelMonitor’s DefaultModelMonitor with a custom constraints JSON specifying the allowed 20% change for device_type categories and schedule frequent jobs.
answers.B: Implement a Kinesis Data Analytics job to maintain real-time category counts and compare to training counts.
answers.C: Use Clarify’s bias monitor to set fair thresholds on device_type representation.
answers.D: Capture endpoint inputs to S3 and run a daily Athena job to compute ratios and alert.

explanation: A is correct because DefaultModelMonitor constraints allow category-level drift threshold configuration, scheduled regularly. B and D are custom. C is misusing bias monitor, not intended for drift constraints.

stem: An automotive company uses real-time inference for predictive maintenance. They must validate that all required sensor fields exist and log any missing fields for further investigation, without failing invocations. How should they set this up?

answers.A: Implement input validation in the inference container code and reject requests with missing fields.
answers.B: Use ModelMonitor’s default data quality monitor to reject invocations with missing fields.
answers.C: Stream inference input logs to CloudWatch Logs and create metrics filters for missing fields.
answers.D: Configure ModelMonitor with a custom preprocessor script that checks for missing keys, logs violations to S3, and does not block the endpoint.

explanation: D is correct: ModelMonitor’s preprocessor can implement validation logic, log violations, and does not interfere with real-time endpoint behavior. A blocks requests. B cannot reject invocations. C requires log parsing and has delay.

stem: A travel app’s SageMaker real-time endpoint is scaled to multiple instances for high traffic. They need aggregated abnormalities in feature distributions across all instances. Which configuration ensures correct drift detection?

answers.A: Deploy a monitor job per instance capturing to instance-specific S3 prefixes and aggregate results in Athena.
answers.B: Enable DataCaptureConfig at the endpoint level to collect across all instances, and run a single ModelMonitor job on that capture location.
answers.C: Add a sidecar container per instance to forward data to Kinesis Data Streams for drift detection.
answers.D: Use CloudWatch metrics on each instance and manually compute distribution shifts in a Lambda.

explanation: B is correct: DataCaptureConfig at endpoint level automatically aggregates across instances. A is complex. C and D require additional infrastructure and custom aggregation.

stem: A gaming platform has an endpoint for matchmaking that logs into DynamoDB. They need to monitor that output predictions are within the valid score range [0,1] and alert if outliers appear. Which solution is optimal?

answers.A: Schedule a ModelMonitor default data quality job with constraints JSON specifying numeric_validity for the output_score feature and set CloudWatch alarms.
answers.B: Use Lambda streams on DynamoDB to check each output and publish custom CloudWatch metrics for out-of-range values.
answers.C: Enable Amazon Kinesis Firehose on logs to S3 and run nightly Athena queries to detect out-of-range values.
answers.D: Instrument application code to validate scores before writing and send alerts via SNS.

explanation: A is correct: ModelMonitor constraints support numeric validity checks and integrate with alarms. B and C are custom solutions more maintenance. D moves monitoring into application logic rather than production monitoring.

stem: A retailer’s real-time pricing endpoint serves dynamic pricing. They want to test periodically whether price predictions exceed a profit margin threshold and revert if they do. Which monitoring feature should they use?

answers.A: Use ModelQualityMonitor with a custom metric that computes profit margin on predictions.
answers.B: Schedule a Lambda to call the endpoint, compute profit margin, and alarm.
answers.C: Use ModelMonitor’s output constraints JSON to define the profit margin threshold on prediction and schedule continuous monitoring.
answers.D: Implement profit margin check logic in the inference container and emit CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: C is correct: ModelMonitor supports output constraints for predictions and continuous monitoring. A is misusing quality monitor, which focuses on ground truth comparison. B and D are custom implementations requiring more code.

stem: An insurance provider uses a batch inference pipeline on S3 with predictions and claims. They need to identify when the ratio of denied claims to total predictions deviates by more than 15% from the baseline. Which tool and configuration do they choose?

answers.A: Use Clarify ModelBiasMonitor with a custom preprocessor to compute the ratio and schedule daily.
answers.B: Use ModelQualityMonitor with ground truth and predictions, define a custom violation report with denied_claims/total and threshold, and schedule daily runs.
answers.C: Use DefaultModelMonitor data quality for this ratio and set thresholds.
answers.D: Query S3 via Athena daily to compute the ratio and call a Step Functions pipeline.

explanation: B is correct: ModelQualityMonitor supports custom metrics for model performance comparisons, including custom functions like ratio of denied claims. A is bias monitor, not for performance metrics. C is data quality; D is custom.

stem: A sports analytics firm needs to detect if the distribution of a continuous feature ‘player_speed’ starts trending downward in real-time endpoint predictions. They require a rolling window of last 1,000 inferences. How can they configure Model Monitor?

answers.A: Set DataCaptureConfig, configure a monitoring schedule with monitoring_interval=1 minute, and set sampling_percentage so that window size approximates 1,000. Use constraints on the mean of player_speed.
answers.B: Enable Clarify drift detector with window_size=1000 for player_speed.
answers.C: Stream inference outputs to Kinesis Data Streams and configure Kinesis Analytics to compute rolling averages.
answers.D: Use a Lambda triggered on capture S3 events to maintain a sliding window in DynamoDB and trigger alarms.

explanation: A is correct: monitoring_interval and sampling_percentage controls sample size per job; constraints can specify mean thresholds. B is not built-in. C and D are custom solutions outside Model Monitor.

stem: A medical imaging application serves predictions for tumor detection. For compliance, any missing license_plate field (erroneously included) must be detected at inference time and reported, but not block inference. Which Model Monitor component is appropriate?

answers.A: Use DefaultModelMonitor data quality monitor to enforce presence of license_plate.
answers.B: Use ModelExplainabilityMonitor to detect missing features.
answers.C: Use ModelQualityMonitor comparing ground truth, specifying missing field detection.
answers.D: Use a custom preprocessor script in ModelMonitor constraints to check for license_plate existence and log violations.

explanation: D is correct: a preprocessor script can validate arbitrary conditions (including extraneous fields) without affecting inference. A does not support arbitrary missing field checks. B and C are for explainability and performance respectively.

stem: An ad-tech firm runs real-time bidding predictions and must detect when the click-through rate (CTR) predicted by the model deviates by more than 10% from training CTR. They have no ground truth in real time. What feature of SageMaker solves this?

answers.A: Use ModelQualityMonitor with placeholders for ground truth CTR.
answers.B: Use ModelMonitor’s custom reporter in data quality to compute predicted CTR distribution drift against baseline.
answers.C: Use Clarify bias monitor to detect prediction bias on CTR.
answers.D: Use endpoint logs and Athena to compute CTR distribution daily.

explanation: B is correct: data quality monitors can compute statistics on predictions alone, enabling detection of predicted CTR shifts without ground truth. A is not applicable since quality monitor requires ground truth. C misuses bias monitor. D is custom and offline.

stem: A gaming platform needs to ensure that inference payload sizes don’t suddenly increase (which could indicate malicious inputs). They want to monitor payload byte size distributions in production. How can they achieve this?

answers.A: Use DefaultModelMonitor with a preprocessor script to compute payload size feature, set constraints on the size distribution, and schedule monitoring.
answers.B: Modify inference container to log payload size to CloudWatch and alarm on spikes.
answers.C: Use Lambda triggered on S3 capture PUT events to record object sizes and alert.
answers.D: Write a Kinesis Data Analytics job to analyze payload streams for size anomalies.

explanation: A is correct: ModelMonitor allows custom features via preprocessor scripts (including payload size) and constraint definitions. B, C, D require separate pipelines and custom code.

stem: A supply chain model produces predictions every minute. The team must compute the percentage of predictions greater than threshold X and alert if it falls below 30% for more than 10 minutes. They have Model Monitor enabled. What is the simplest way to implement?

answers.A: Use Clarify’s bias monitor to configure threshold checks on prediction distribution.
answers.B: Schedule a daily ModelQualityMonitor job with custom metrics file for percentage above X.
answers.C: Configure a real-time ModelMonitor schedule with a custom constraints JSON to compute % above X and set alarms on violations every 5 minutes.
answers.D: Stream predictions to Kinesis Data Streams and use AWS Lambda to monitor percentage.

explanation: C is correct: ModelMonitor constraints support custom aggregations (like percentage above threshold) and real-time schedules. A and B misapply Clarify or daily quality jobs. D is custom and more complex.

stem: A biotech lab uses an asynchronous SageMaker endpoint. They need to monitor and alert on both input data completeness and response time exceeding 2 seconds for each batch. Which combination of Model Monitor capabilities achieves this?

answers.A: Enable DataCaptureConfig for request and response, configure DefaultModelMonitor with separate data quality and custom latency constraints, schedule every 5 minutes.
answers.B: Use Clarify ModelExplainabilityMonitor for input completeness and CloudWatch metrics for latency.
answers.C: Use two separate Lambda functions—one reading S3 captures for missing fields and one alarm on CloudWatch latency metrics.
answers.D: Run a daily ModelQualityMonitor job to measure completeness and latency metrics.

explanation: A is correct because DefaultModelMonitor can validate data quality and custom metrics like latency in one job. B misuses explainability. C is custom. D is too infrequent.

stem: A financial firm wants to monitor covariance drift between two features, income and expenditure, in real-time inference data. Which Model Monitor strategy accomplishes this?

answers.A: Use Clarify bias detector to compute covariance and schedule monitoring.
answers.B: Schedule Athena queries to compute covariance and trigger alarms.
answers.C: Implement a custom preprocessor in ModelMonitor to compute covariance drift constraint and schedule frequent runs.
answers.D: Stream inference data to Redshift and run SQL to compute covariance daily.

explanation: C is correct: custom preprocessor scripts in ModelMonitor allow computing covariance and enforcing drift constraints. A and B don’t natively compute covariance. D is custom and offline.

stem: A mobile app uses a SageMaker real-time endpoint. They want to detect if any string feature contains non-UTF8 characters in production. Which approach is most maintainable?

answers.A: Modify inference code to reject non-UTF8 inputs and log violations.
answers.B: Use Clarify’s bias detector to detect invalid characters.
answers.C: Run a Lambda on captured S3 data to search for invalid encodings.
answers.D: Configure ModelMonitor with a custom preprocessor to scan string features for non-UTF8 and log violations in S3.

explanation: D is correct: ModelMonitor preprocessor scripts can perform arbitrary validation (e.g., encoding checks) with minimal maintenance and decoupled from inference code. A couples monitoring with serving. B is misapplied. C is custom.

stem: A retailer uses batch transform to score customer churn nightly. They need to verify that output probabilities sum to 1 for each record (softmax outputs) and alert on any anomalies. Which Model Monitor feature supports this at lowest operational cost?

answers.A: Use Clarify bias monitor to validate output probability sums.
answers.B: Use DefaultModelMonitor with a custom postprocessor script to compute sum of probabilities per record and set constraints that sum equals 1.
answers.C: Instrument batch transform container to raise errors when sums differ and notify via SNS.
answers.D: Write Athena query over output files to check sums and send alerts.

explanation: B is correct: postprocessor scripts in ModelMonitor can validate prediction outputs and enforce numeric constraints. A is misapplied. C and D require custom code or queries.

stem: A manufacturing line inference endpoint outputs categorical defect labels. They must detect when a rare defect category appears more than twice in an hour, indicating a quality issue. How can they configure Model Monitor?

answers.A: Create a DefaultModelMonitor job with custom constraints specifying max_count=2 for that category over a 1-hour window and schedule jobs accordingly.
answers.B: Run a Clarify bias monitor to detect changes in rare label frequency.
answers.C: Use Kinesis Data Streams to aggregate counts and Lambda to alert.
answers.D: Schedule daily Athena queries on captured data to check counts.

explanation: A is correct: ModelMonitor supports frequency constraints for categorical values. B misuses bias. C and D are custom and less real-time.

stem: An app uses a SageMaker real-time endpoint for language translation. They want to ensure that none of the translated outputs contain profane words. Which Model Monitor mechanism should they use?

answers.A: Use Clarify bias monitor with a profanity lexicon.
answers.B: Modify inference code to filter profanity and report.
answers.C: Configure ModelMonitor with a custom postprocessor script that scans outputs against a profanity list and logs violations.
answers.D: Stream responses to Kinesis and run a profanity detection Lambda.

explanation: C is correct: postprocessor scripts in ModelMonitor can implement content validation and integrate with alerts. A is misused. B couples monitoring into serving. D requires extra infrastructure.

stem: A logistics service uses a multi-model endpoint for forecasting. They need per-model latency and feature distribution monitoring. The endpoint metadata tags each invocation with model_id. How can they implement this in ModelMonitor?

answers.A: Enable separate DataCaptureConfig per model_id by deploying multiple endpoints.
answers.B: Enable a single DataCaptureConfig that captures model_id in payload, schedule ModelMonitor with a group_by based on model_id for both latency and data quality metrics.
answers.C: Stream all invocations to Kinesis Data Streams, use a Lambda to split by model_id.
answers.D: Deploy Clarify bias detectors per model for distribution monitoring.

explanation: B is correct: ModelMonitor supports group_by functionality on a specified feature (model_id) to generate separate metrics per group. A duplicates endpoints. C is custom. D misuses bias detectors.

stem: A financial services company needs to detect fraudulent transactions in real time with sub-50ms latency per transaction, while also running nightly trend analyses on aggregated data. They plan separate ML pipelines for each use case. Which combination of inferencing types should they implement?

answers.A: Batch inferencing for fraud detection and real-time inferencing for trend analysis
answers.B: Real-time inferencing for fraud detection and batch inferencing for trend analysis
answers.C: Streaming inferencing for fraud detection and online inferencing for trend analysis
answers.D: Online inferencing for fraud detection and micro-batch inferencing for trend analysis

explanation: Real-time inferencing meets sub-50ms latency for fraud detection; batch inferencing is appropriate for nightly aggregate trend analysis. Streaming and micro-batch are not AWS inference categories defined in this context.

stem: An e-commerce team is deciding between logistic regression and random forest for a binary classification task. They refer to these as “algorithms.” After training, they obtain predictive artifacts they deploy. In AWS terms, what is the term for these deployed artifacts?

answers.A: Hyperparameters
answers.B: Features
answers.C: Models
answers.D: Labels

explanation: Algorithms (logistic regression, random forest) produce trained artifacts called models. Hyperparameters configure algorithms; features are inputs; labels are outputs used during training.

stem: A manufacturing firm collects sensor readings (temperature, vibration, pressure) every second as JSON messages and also attaches operator comments as free text. What best describes the types of data ingested?

answers.A: Structured tabular data only
answers.B: Unstructured multimedia data
answers.C: Semi-structured numerical data only
answers.D: Mixed structured (numeric) and unstructured (text) data

explanation: Numeric sensor readings are structured; operator comments are unstructured text. It’s mixed. The other options mischaracterize the combination.

stem: A marketing team wants to segment customers by purchase behavior without any predefined labels. They plan to discover latent groups. Which learning paradigm should they apply?

answers.A: Supervised classification
answers.B: Unsupervised clustering
answers.C: Reinforcement learning
answers.D: Semi-supervised learning

explanation: Clustering on unlabeled data is unsupervised learning. Supervised requires labels; reinforcement uses rewards; semi-supervised mixes labels and unlabeled data.

stem: A logistics company uses trial and error and a reward function to optimize warehouse pick-and-place operations in simulation. Which ML method are they using?

answers.A: Supervised learning
answers.B: Unsupervised learning
answers.C: Reinforcement learning
answers.D: Self-supervised learning

explanation: Using a reward signal in simulation for actions is reinforcement learning. Supervised uses labeled examples; unsupervised finds patterns without rewards; self-supervised derives labels internally but not via reward.

stem: An image classification solution on AWS uses a convolutional neural network with millions of parameters and requires GPUs. Which term best categorizes this approach?

answers.A: Deep learning
answers.B: Traditional ML algorithm
answers.C: Reinforcement learning agent
answers.D: Ensemble tree model

explanation: CNNs with many layers/functions on unstructured images are deep learning. Ensemble trees and traditional ML do not generally use deep neural nets; reinforcement learning uses a reward model.

stem: A research group selects a pre-trained language model of 20B parameters that supports few-shot prompting. What terminology best describes this artifact?

answers.A: A neural network
answers.B: A supervised model
answers.C: An embedding
answers.D: A large language model (LLM)

explanation: A pre-trained model with billions of parameters for language tasks is an LLM. While it is a neural network and supervised pre-training is used, the specific term is LLM; embeddings are vector representations.

stem: A facial recognition model misclassifies certain demographics more often than others. What term describes this issue?

answers.A: Bias
answers.B: Variance
answers.C: Fit
answers.D: Regularization

explanation: Systematic error disadvantaging particular groups is bias. Variance relates to sensitivity to data fluctuations; fit/reg. concern under/overfitting and penalty terms respectively.

stem: A text classification model achieves 99% accuracy on training data but only 60% on new customer emails. Which problem is occurring?

answers.A: High bias
answers.B: Data leakage
answers.C: Underfitting
answers.D: Overfitting

explanation: A large gap between training and test performance indicates overfitting. High bias or underfitting would show poor performance on both. Data leakage would inflate test performance, not reduce it sharply.

stem: An online retailer deploys a model endpoint to score customer propensity in milliseconds per request. Which term describes this stage?

answers.A: Model training
answers.B: Feature engineering
answers.C: Inference
answers.D: Data preprocessing

explanation: Serving a deployed model to generate predictions is inference. Training builds the model; feature engineering and preprocessing occur before model usage.

stem: A shipping firm wants to detect package damage by analyzing shipment photos. Which AI domain should they leverage?

answers.A: Computer vision
answers.B: Natural language processing
answers.C: Reinforcement learning
answers.D: Speech recognition

explanation: Analyzing images falls under computer vision. NLP handles text; reinforcement learning uses rewards; speech recognition handles audio.

stem: A call center wants to transcribe and analyze customer audio for sentiment. Which AI domain and subtask are involved?

answers.A: Computer vision with OCR
answers.B: Computer vision with object detection
answers.C: Natural language processing with speech-to-text and sentiment analysis
answers.D: Reinforcement learning with audio encoding

explanation: Transcribing speech is speech-to-text (an NLP subtask) followed by sentiment analysis (also NLP). The other options misapply computer vision or reinforcement learning to audio.

stem: A startup uses customer behavior logs to train a model and wants to evaluate various algorithms efficiently. Which pipeline step does this describe?

answers.A: Deployment
answers.B: Experimentation (training and validation)
answers.C: Feature storage
answers.D: Data annotation

explanation: Testing multiple algorithms with validation data is experimentation within the training lifecycle. Deployment comes after; feature storage and annotation are different steps.

stem: A dataset contains numeric, categorical, text, image, and time-series fields. How would you classify this dataset overall?

answers.A: Structured
answers.B: Unstructured
answers.C: Semi-structured
answers.D: Heterogeneous multimodal data

explanation: Multiple data modalities (numeric, text, image, time-series) define heterogeneous multimodal data. Structured/unstructured/semi-structured don’t capture multiple distinct modalities.

stem: A credit scoring model uses decision trees and logistic regression, then blends outputs. What ensemble method category is this?

answers.A: Stacking
answers.B: Bagging
answers.C: Boosting
answers.D: Blending

explanation: Combining diverse model outputs via a meta-learner is stacking. Bagging uses same algorithm on subsets; boosting sequentially focuses on errors; blending is a holdout variant of stacking but less formal.

stem: A medical imaging model needs 3D scans and uses volumetric convolution. Which architectural choice defines this model?

answers.A: Recurrent neural network
answers.B: Transformer
answers.C: Autoencoder
answers.D: 3D convolutional neural network

explanation: 3D CNNs handle volumetric data via 3D convolutions. RNNs process sequences; transformers use attention; autoencoders learn embeddings.

stem: When splitting data for training and inference, which data characteristic ensures the model generalizes?

answers.A: High label imbalance
answers.B: Representative i.i.d. distribution
answers.C: Missing values集中
answers.D: Highly correlated features

explanation: An independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) split ensures the inference data resemble training data. Label imbalance, missing values, or correlated features hamper generalization.

stem: A recommender system logs user clicks and ratings. Which learning paradigm uses both past actions and reward signals to improve suggestions?

answers.A: Unsupervised learning
answers.B: Supervised learning
answers.C: Reinforcement learning
answers.D: Self-supervised learning

explanation: A recommender optimizing using click/reward feedback is reinforcement learning. Supervised uses explicit labels; unsupervised finds patterns; self-supervised generates labels.

stem: A startup fine-tunes a pre-trained transformer-based LLM by updating all weights on domain data. What process are they performing?

answers.A: Prompt engineering
answers.B: Fine-tuning
answers.C: Inference
answers.D: Embedding

explanation: Updating model weights on new data is fine-tuning. Prompt engineering crafts inputs; inference uses the model; embedding produces vector representations.

stem: A dataset of customer addresses stored as JSON documents without fixed schema is an example of which data type?

answers.A: Structured
answers.B: Unstructured
answers.C: Semi-structured
answers.D: Multimodal

explanation: JSON documents with flexible schema are semi-structured. Structured implies rigid tables; unstructured refers to raw text/images; multimodal combines multiple media types.

stem: A deep network’s capacity to memorize training noise rather than general patterns relates to which property?

answers.A: Bias
answers.B: Fairness
answers.C: Regularization
answers.D: Variance

explanation: High variance indicates sensitivity to noise and overfitting. Bias relates to systematic error; fairness to equity; regularization is a technique to reduce variance.

stem: A supply-chain model uses past demand to predict next-month orders via linear regression. Which algorithm type is this?

answers.A: Regression
answers.B: Classification
answers.C: Clustering
answers.D: Dimensionality reduction

explanation: Predicting a continuous numeric target is regression. Classification predicts discrete labels; clustering groups unlabeled data; dimensionality reduction reduces feature space.

stem: An NLP pipeline transforms text into 768-dimension vectors before clustering. What are these vectors called?

answers.A: Features
answers.B: Embeddings
answers.C: Hyperparameters
answers.D: Parameters

explanation: Embeddings are dense vector representations of text. Features are inputs to models; parameters are learned weights; hyperparameters configure training.

stem: A governance team audits a model’s training algorithm and discovered inconsistent outputs for identical inputs across runs. Which concept might explain this?

answers.A: High bias
answers.B: Data imbalance
answers.C: Nondeterministic initialization
answers.D: Overfitting

explanation: Random weight initialization or nondeterministic operations in deep learning can lead to different outputs for identical inputs. Bias, imbalance, and overfitting don’t directly cause run-to-run variability.

stem: A customer service chatbot uses a model that responds within seconds but batches billing analysis nightly. How should you label these two inferencing modes?

answers.A: Synchronous and asynchronous inferencing
answers.B: Online and offline training
answers.C: Real-time and streaming inferencing
answers.D: Real-time and batch inferencing

explanation: Chatbot responses require real-time (online) inference; nightly billing analysis is batch inference. The other terms mix training with inference or streaming, which is not the defined mode here.

stem: An ML pipeline scales behavior analysis to new data without labels by learning data structure. Which technique applies?

answers.A: Supervised classification
answers.B: Unsupervised learning
answers.C: Reinforcement learning
answers.D: Transfer learning

explanation: Unsupervised learning discovers patterns in unlabeled data. Transfer learning uses labeled source domains; reinforcement learning uses rewards; classification is supervised.

stem: A text summarization system must compress long documents into key sentences. Which AI subfield does this represent?

answers.A: Computer vision
answers.B: Reinforcement learning
answers.C: Natural language processing
answers.D: Anomaly detection

explanation: Summarization is an NLP task. Computer vision processes images; reinforcement is reward-based; anomaly detection finds outliers.

stem: A model’s training loop uses gradient descent to minimize a loss function. Which concept does the loss function represent?

answers.A: Algorithm objective
answers.B: Model artifact
answers.C: Feature set
answers.D: Hyperparameter

explanation: The loss function defines the objective the algorithm optimizes. The model artifact is the trained parameters; features are inputs; hyperparameters configure training.

stem: A pre-training phase on massive text yields a foundation model that can be specialized later. What is the general process called?

answers.A: Inference
answers.B: Pre-training
answers.C: Fine-tuning
answers.D: Evaluation

explanation: Pre-training on large unlabeled corpora yields a foundation model. Fine-tuning specializes; inference uses the model; evaluation measures performance.

stem: A wildlife monitoring project clusters animal tracks without labels and then assigns species names manually to clusters. Which workflow combines the two learning types?

answers.A: Supervised learning
answers.B: Reinforcement learning
answers.C: Unsupervised learning
answers.D: Semi-supervised learning

explanation: They initially use unsupervised clustering then manually label clusters, combining labeled and unlabeled data = semi-supervised. Pure supervised or unsupervised use only one type; reinforcement uses rewards.

stem: A model’s performance degrades over time because data distribution shifts. Which concept describes this challenge?

answers.A: Overfitting
answers.B: Data drift
answers.C: Bias
answers.D: Variance

explanation: Data drift refers to changes in input data distribution over time, causing degradation. Bias/variance relate to model errors; overfitting is memorization.

stem: A dataset has 100 features but you observe diminishing returns beyond 10 in model performance. Which concept are you examining?

answers.A: Regularization strength
answers.B: Algorithm complexity
answers.C: Feature importance
answers.D: Model capacity

explanation: Evaluating how adding features impacts performance assesses feature importance. Regularization, algorithm complexity, and model capacity address other aspects.

stem: A retail company wants to segment customers based on purchasing behavior to tailor marketing campaigns. They have numerical features such as purchase frequency, average order value, and days since last purchase. Which ML technique and AWS service combination best suits this use case?

answers.A: Use the built-in K-Means clustering algorithm in Amazon SageMaker to group customers.
answers.B: Use Amazon Personalize to automatically cluster customers and generate segments.
answers.C: Use sentiment analysis in Amazon Comprehend to segment customers by sentiment.
answers.D: Use Amazon Forecast to predict future customer segments over time.

explanation: Unsupervised clustering via SageMaker K-Means is ideal for grouping based on numeric behavior; other services are for recommendations, sentiment, or forecasting.

stem: A fintech startup needs to identify potentially fraudulent credit card transactions in real time with minimal ML expertise and wants pre-trained fraud detection capabilities. Which AWS service should they choose?

answers.A: Amazon Fraud Detector
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
answers.C: Amazon Comprehend
answers.D: Amazon GuardDuty

explanation: Amazon Fraud Detector provides domain-specific, pre-trained models for fraud detection; others are for labeling, NLP, or threat detection.

stem: A global brand wants to analyze customer tweets to gauge public sentiment about a new product launch without building or training custom models. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend Sentiment Analysis
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker BlazingText
answers.C: Amazon Translate
answers.D: Amazon Lex

explanation: Comprehend’s built-in sentiment API analyzes text sentiment directly; other services are for custom text models, translation, or chatbots.

stem: A media company needs to convert recorded webinar audio into text transcripts to index content for search. Which AWS service should they choose?

answers.A: Amazon Transcribe
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend
answers.C: Amazon Polly
answers.D: Amazon Translate

explanation: Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text; Comprehend analyzes text, Polly generates speech, Translate translates text.

stem: An e-commerce website must provide real-time translation of product descriptions into multiple languages to serve global customers. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon Translate
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend
answers.C: Amazon Polly
answers.D: Amazon Lex

explanation: Amazon Translate provides real-time neural translation; Comprehend is for NLP analysis, Polly for speech, Lex for conversational interfaces.

stem: A legal firm wants to automatically extract key phrases and entities (like person, organization, date) from large volumes of contracts. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend Entity and Key Phrase Extraction
answers.B: Amazon Textract Table Extraction
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker BlazingText
answers.D: Amazon Kendra

explanation: Comprehend extracts entities and key phrases; Textract focuses on form/ table OCR, SageMaker needs model building, Kendra is search.

stem: A news app needs to generate audio versions of articles for accessibility. Which AWS service should they integrate?

answers.A: Amazon Transcribe
answers.B: Amazon Translate
answers.C: Amazon Polly
answers.D: Amazon Lex

explanation: Amazon Polly converts text to lifelike speech; Transcribe converts speech to text, Translate translates text, Lex builds chat interfaces.

stem: A company wants to build a conversational agent to answer common HR policy questions via chat. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend
answers.B: Amazon Lex (without Lambda integration)
answers.C: Amazon Polly
answers.D: Amazon Lex with intent management

explanation: Amazon Lex provides NLU, intent handling, and conversation flow; Comprehend is for text analysis, Polly for TTS.

stem: An online retailer wants to offer personalized product recommendations based on browsing behavior and purchase history. Which AWS service is most suitable?

answers.A: Amazon Personalize
answers.B: Amazon Forecast
answers.C: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
answers.D: Amazon Personalize

explanation: Amazon Personalize is designed for personalized recommendations; Forecast is forecasting, Kinesis analyzes streaming data but not personalized models.

stem: A manufacturing firm needs to automatically detect defects in product images on the assembly line. They need bounding boxes around defects. Which service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon Rekognition Text Detection
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker Image Classification
answers.C: Amazon Textract
answers.D: Amazon Rekognition Object Detection

explanation: Rekognition’s object detection provides bounding boxes; image classification labels whole images, Textract is OCR.

stem: A bank wants to build a model to predict customer churn probability using historical account activity. Which ML technique and AWS service should they choose?

answers.A: Binary classification using SageMaker built-in XGBoost algorithm
answers.B: Unsupervised K-Means clustering in Amazon SageMaker
answers.C: Reinforcement learning in AWS DeepRacer
answers.D: Time series forecasting in Amazon Forecast

explanation: Predicting churn is a supervised binary classification problem; SageMaker’s XGBoost is appropriate.

stem: A telecom operator wants to forecast next-month data usage per customer to provision network capacity. Which technique and AWS service best apply?

answers.A: Classification with SageMaker Linear Learner
answers.B: Time series forecasting with Amazon Forecast
answers.C: Clustering with SageMaker K-Means
answers.D: Anomaly detection with SageMaker Random Cut Forest

explanation: Forecasting numeric usage over time requires time series forecasting; Amazon Forecast is purpose-built.

stem: A logistics company receives IoT sensor data and wants to detect abnormal temperature spikes without labeled anomalies. Which AWS service and algorithm combination should they use?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner
answers.B: Amazon Fraud Detector
answers.C: Amazon Comprehend
answers.D: SageMaker Random Cut Forest anomaly detection

explanation: Random Cut Forest in SageMaker unsupervised algorithm detects anomalies in unlabeled time series.

stem: An educational platform wants to cluster quiz questions based on topic similarity using NLP embeddings. They don’t require supervised labels. Which approach is most appropriate?

answers.A: Use Amazon Translate then cluster translated text
answers.B: Use Amazon Comprehend sentiment scores
answers.C: Generate embeddings with SageMaker JumpStart BERT model and cluster via K-Means
answers.D: Use Amazon Personalize grouping

explanation: Extracting embeddings with a pre-trained model then K-Means clustering is an unsupervised NLP approach.

stem: A marketing team considers using ML to map postal codes to region names because there are only 50 unique codes. Is ML appropriate here?

answers.A: Yes – use Amazon SageMaker lookup table training
answers.B: No – use a simple rule-based lookup table (no ML)
answers.C: Yes – use Amazon Comprehend to infer regions
answers.D: No – use Amazon Forecast to predict region mapping

explanation: Mapping a small finite set is best solved with a rule-based lookup, not ML.

stem: A company wants to detect specific keywords in customer call transcriptions to trigger alerts. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabulary and AWS Lambda keyword filter
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend Key Phrase Extraction
answers.C: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
answers.D: Amazon Lex Slot Filling

explanation: Custom vocabulary in Transcribe captures keywords in speech-to-text, Lambda filters them; Comprehend extracts after text conversion.

stem: An HR department needs to automatically categorize resume documents by skill sets using pre-built models and minimal customization. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker BlazingText
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend Custom Classification
answers.C: Amazon Textract form analysis
answers.D: Amazon Personalize

explanation: Comprehend Custom Classification allows rapid text classification with minimal model building; others are for embeddings, OCR, or recommendations.

stem: A legal team needs to redact personally identifiable information (PII) from scanned PDF contracts. Which AWS service or combination should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend PII detection alone
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker DocumentClassifier
answers.C: Amazon Textract for OCR then Comprehend PII detection
answers.D: Amazon Rekognition Text Moderation

explanation: Textract extracts text from scanned PDFs; Comprehend PII API then identifies and redacts PII.

stem: An online gaming company wants to recommend in-game items based on player behavior and contextual metadata. Which AWS service should they choose?

answers.A: Amazon Personalize
answers.B: Amazon Forecast
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker Neo
answers.D: Amazon Comprehend

explanation: Personalize builds contextual, real-time recommendation models; Forecast is for time series, Neo for deployment, Comprehend for NLP.

stem: A pharmaceutical company wants to group patients into cohorts for a clinical trial based on lab results and demographic features without labeled outcomes. Which ML technique applies?

answers.A: Supervised classification using SageMaker XGBoost
answers.B: Unsupervised clustering using SageMaker K-Means
answers.C: Reinforcement learning using Amazon SageMaker RL agents
answers.D: Anomaly detection using SageMaker Random Cut Forest

explanation: Clustering groups data without labels into cohorts; supervised or anomaly detection are less appropriate.

stem: A contact center wants to route incoming chats based on detected customer intent without building custom ML models. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Lex V2 with custom code
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend Syntax Analysis
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker DeepAR
answers.D: Amazon Lex built-in intent classification

explanation: Lex provides built-in intent classification for chat routing; other services are for syntax, forecasting, or require custom ML.

stem: A bank wants to estimate credit risk score as a continuous variable from customer profiles. Which ML technique and AWS service combination is best?

answers.A: Unsupervised clustering with SageMaker K-Means
answers.B: Anomaly detection with SageMaker Random Cut Forest
answers.C: Regression using SageMaker Linear Learner
answers.D: Classification using Amazon Fraud Detector

explanation: Predicting a continuous risk score is regression; SageMaker Linear Learner supports regression tasks.

stem: A manufacturing plant collects vibration data and suspects rare equipment failures. They have no labeled failure examples. Which AWS approach should they use?

answers.A: Supervised classification in Amazon SageMaker
answers.B: Unsupervised anomaly detection using SageMaker Random Cut Forest
answers.C: Time series forecasting using Amazon Forecast
answers.D: Clustering using SageMaker K-Means

explanation: Unsupervised anomaly detection detects rare failures without labeled data; clustering groups all data equally.

stem: A travel website wants to extract flight numbers, dates, and passenger names from PDF itineraries. Which AWS service combination should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend Entities API
answers.B: Amazon Textract Forms API only
answers.C: Amazon Textract for OCR then Amazon Comprehend Entity Extraction
answers.D: Amazon SageMaker OCR built-in model

explanation: Textract OCRs form data; Comprehend extracts structured entities; other options miss one stage.

stem: A social media analytics firm needs to cluster trending topics without prior labels. They want to use embeddings from a pre-trained language model. Which AWS service should they leverage?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend Topic Modeling
answers.B: SageMaker JumpStart transformer embeddings + K-Means
answers.C: Amazon Personalize clustering
answers.D: Amazon Rekognition for topic detection

explanation: JumpStart provides pre-trained models for embeddings; clustering then groups topics; Comprehend doesn’t expose topic modeling.

stem: A chatbot needs to answer customer queries by matching to FAQ entries. They require semantic matching rather than keyword matching. Which AWS service/model approach should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Lex with keyword slots
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend sentiment analysis
answers.C: Amazon Translate semantic matching
answers.D: Generate embeddings using SageMaker JumpStart and perform similarity search

explanation: Embeddings and similarity search provide semantic matching; other services are for keyword, sentiment, or translation.

stem: A publisher wants to detect the language of submitted articles automatically before translation. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend DetectDominantLanguage
answers.B: Amazon Translate language detection
answers.C: Amazon Polly language identification
answers.D: Amazon Transcribe language model

explanation: Comprehend’s DetectDominantLanguage API identifies text language; Translate focuses on translation post-detection.

stem: An agriculture startup gathers drone imagery to identify crop health issues automatically. They need object detection and classification. Which AWS service combination is suitable?

answers.A: Amazon Rekognition Text Detection + Comprehend
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker K-Means clustering
answers.C: Amazon Textract Table Extraction
answers.D: Amazon SageMaker Object Detection built-in algorithm

explanation: SageMaker’s Object Detection algorithm (e.g., SSD) supports bounding boxes and classification in imagery.

stem: A legal department wants to determine sentiment trends in case law documents over time and highlight emerging negative topics. Which AWS services should they combine?

answers.A: Amazon Textract + Amazon Translate
answers.B: Amazon Comprehend Key Phrases + Amazon Personalize
answers.C: Amazon Textract for OCR + Amazon Comprehend Sentiment Analysis + Amazon QuickSight for visualization
answers.D: Amazon Rekognition + Amazon Athena

explanation: Textract extracts text, Comprehend analyzes sentiment, QuickSight visualizes trends; others mismatch functions.

stem: A retailer wants to forecast daily sales volume per store for the next quarter, incorporating holiday effects and promotions. Which AWS solution should they choose?

answers.A: Regression with SageMaker XGBoost
answers.B: Time series forecasting with Amazon Forecast
answers.C: Clustering with SageMaker K-Means
answers.D: Anomaly detection with SageMaker Random Cut Forest

explanation: Forecast incorporates seasonality and holiday effects; regression would require manual feature engineering.

stem: A health app records user vitals and needs to detect abnormal patterns in real time for alerting. They have streaming data and no labeled anomalies. Which AWS combination is best?

answers.A: Amazon Forecast streaming predictions
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner streaming inference
answers.C: Amazon Fraud Detector real-time API
answers.D: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics to ingest + SageMaker Random Cut Forest for anomaly detection

explanation: Kinesis ingests streaming data; SageMaker RCF analyzes unlabeled anomalies in real time.

stem: A company has a dataset of customer emails and wants to route them to the correct department automatically. They need intent classification out of the box. Which AWS service should they use?

answers.A: Amazon Comprehend Custom Classification
answers.B: Amazon SageMaker Object Detection
answers.C: Amazon Translate
answers.D: Amazon Personalize

explanation: Comprehend Custom Classification provides easy training for text routing; other services are irrelevant.

stem: A startup wants to create a voice-driven assistant that transcribes speech, interprets intent, and responds vocally. Which combination of AWS services is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon Transcribe + Amazon Comprehend + Amazon Polly
answers.B: Amazon Transcribe -> Amazon Lex -> Amazon Polly
answers.C: Amazon Lex -> Amazon Translate -> Amazon Comprehend
answers.D: Amazon Polly -> Amazon SageMaker RL

explanation: Transcribe handles speech-to-text, Lex interprets intent, Polly synthesizes speech; other chains mix stages incorrectly.

stem: A team needs to ensure that feature transformations applied during model training are used identically during real-time inference to avoid training/serving skew. Which AWS service or feature best satisfies this requirement?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
answers.B: AWS Glue DataBrew
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler flow exports
answers.D: Embedding transformations in Lambda functions

explanation: SageMaker Feature Store provides a single source of truth for feature definitions and transformations, ensuring consistency between training and inference. Data Wrangler and Glue cannot serve real-time features, and Lambda-based transformations risk divergence.

stem: You must orchestrate a repeatable end-to-end ML workflow including data preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, and conditional deployment in response to evaluation metrics. Which AWS tool should you choose?

answers.A: AWS Step Functions with custom Lambda tasks
answers.B: AWS Glue Workflows
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines with ConditionStep
answers.D: AWS Data Pipeline

explanation: SageMaker Pipelines natively orchestrates ML steps, supports ConditionStep for metric-based branching, and integrates with training, processing, and model registry. Step Functions and Glue lack ML-specific constructs, and AWS Data Pipeline is deprecated for ML workflows.

stem: A data scientist needs to deploy ten versions of a fraud detection model behind a single endpoint, loading each version only when invoked to minimize memory usage. Which deployment option meets this requirement?

answers.A: Provisioned real-time endpoints per model variant
answers.B: SageMaker serverless endpoint
answers.C: Batch Transform job
answers.D: SageMaker multi-model endpoint

explanation: Multi-model endpoints load models on demand into a container, supporting multiple versions behind a single endpoint. Serverless endpoints cannot host multiple models, and Batch Transform is for offline inference.

stem: To detect input data drift in production, which combination of services and features provides automated baseline generation, continuous monitoring, and alerting?

answers.A: Amazon CloudWatch metrics with custom Lambda evaluations
answers.B: SageMaker Model Monitor’s DataQualityJobDefinition + Amazon EventBridge rule
answers.C: AWS Config with custom rules
answers.D: AWS Glue job scheduled daily

explanation: Model Monitor can generate a baseline from training data (DataQualityJobDefinition), schedule continuous monitoring, and emit results via EventBridge for alerting. Other options require extensive custom work or lack ML-specific drift detection.

stem: Your preprocessing logic involves heavy PySpark transforms on large tabular datasets. Which SageMaker component should you use for scalable, containerized execution?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker Processing with built-in Scikit-learn container
answers.B: AWS Glue ETL job
answers.C: Amazon SageMaker Processing with Spark container
answers.D: AWS Lambda with parallel invocations

explanation: SageMaker Processing supports Spark containers for distributed PySpark workloads within an ML pipeline. Glue is general ETL, not integrated with SageMaker pipelines, and Lambda cannot handle large-scale Spark jobs.

stem: A business requires tracking of every training run’s hyperparameters, input data versions, and evaluation metrics with lineage. Which SageMaker feature is specifically built to capture this metadata?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker Experiments
answers.B: Amazon CloudWatch Logs
answers.C: Amazon S3 object versioning
answers.D: AWS CloudTrail

explanation: SageMaker Experiments records runs, parameters, inputs, and metrics, providing lineage and comparison across trials. CloudWatch Logs and S3 versioning don’t structure ML metadata, and CloudTrail logs only API calls.

stem: When model quality metrics fall below a threshold in production, you need to trigger an automated retraining pipeline. Which architecture best implements this requirement?

answers.A: CloudWatch alarm on endpoint latency to start Lambda
answers.B: AWS Config rule violation to start SageMaker job
answers.C: SNS notification from CloudTrail to trigger training
answers.D: EventBridge rule on Model Monitor alarm to start SageMaker Pipeline

explanation: Model Monitor can detect quality degradation, emit an EventBridge event, and trigger a SageMaker Pipeline that retrains and redeploys the model. Other options don’t tie directly to model quality metrics.

stem: A classification model on a heavily imbalanced dataset shows 95% accuracy but poor minority class detection. Which single metric should you prioritize to better reflect model performance?

answers.A: Overall accuracy
answers.B: Precision
answers.C: F1-score
answers.D: Mean squared error

explanation: F1-score balances precision and recall, and is better suited for imbalanced datasets than accuracy. Precision alone ignores recall, and MSE is for regression.

stem: You want to generate a statistical profile of your training data to serve as a baseline for drift detection. Which SageMaker component accomplishes this with minimal code?

answers.A: SageMaker Clarify bias report
answers.B: SageMaker Model Monitor Data Quality job
answers.C: SageMaker Debugger profiling job
answers.D: SageMaker Edge Manager

explanation: Model Monitor’s DataQualityJobDefinition automatically profiles datasets to generate statistics and constraints used for drift monitoring. Clarify focuses on bias/fairness, Debugger on training diagnostics, Edge Manager on device models.

stem: Your organization needs to track approved model versions and their deployment environments, enabling rollback. Which service should you integrate into your pipeline?

answers.A: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
answers.B: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
answers.C: Amazon DynamoDB
answers.D: AWS CodeCommit

explanation: SageMaker Model Registry manages model versions, approval statuses, and associated metadata, making deployments and rollbacks straightforward. Parameter Store and DynamoDB aren’t specialized for model lifecycle, and CodeCommit is for code, not models.

stem: You need to run custom evaluation code on your test dataset after training completes within the same pipeline. Which SageMaker step type should you use?

answers.A: TrainingStep
answers.B: ProcessingStep
answers.C: TransformStep
answers.D: ModelStep

explanation: ProcessingStep allows execution of arbitrary evaluation scripts post-training and can read model artifacts and test data. TrainingStep only trains, TransformStep performs batch inference, and ModelStep registers a model.

stem: You plan to fine-tune an open-source transformer model from Hugging Face on SageMaker. Which approach minimizes undifferentiated heavy lifting?

answers.A: Use SageMaker Hugging Face DLC via Hugging Face integration
answers.B: Build your own Docker container with Transformers installed
answers.C: Use Amazon EC2 instances with preinstalled Transformers
answers.D: Perform training on AWS Lambda functions

explanation: SageMaker’s built-in Hugging Face deep learning containers provide managed environments and optimization for fine-tuning. Custom containers and EC2 require manual setup, and Lambda cannot handle large training jobs.

stem: Your ML pipeline must decide at runtime whether to continue to deployment based on evaluation metrics. Which SageMaker feature allows you to embed this logic directly in the pipeline definition?

answers.A: Lambda invocation within a Pipeline
answers.B: State Machine integration
answers.C: ConditionStep in SageMaker Pipelines
answers.D: RetryStrategy in TrainingStep

explanation: ConditionStep in SageMaker Pipelines evaluates expressions on step outputs to branch logic without external orchestration. Lambda or Step Functions would decouple, and RetryStrategy only handles retries.

stem: Your service-level agreement requires sub-100ms inference latency at unpredictable traffic volumes for a text classification model. Which SageMaker endpoint type best meets this requirement with minimal management overhead?

answers.A: Multi-model endpoint
answers.B: Serverless inference endpoint
answers.C: Real-time provisioned endpoint
answers.D: Batch transform

explanation: Serverless endpoints automatically scale based on traffic and provide low-latency inference without capacity planning. Real-time provisioned endpoints require manual scaling, multi-model cannot auto-scale, and Batch Transform is offline.

stem: You want to embed feature-engineering code in a pipeline step, reuse it interactively in Data Wrangler, and version control it. Which approach best satisfies these needs?

answers.A: Implement transforms in a Lambda and call from ProcessingStep
answers.B: Write PySpark in a ProcessingStep directly
answers.C: Use Glue DataBrew recipe then export
answers.D: Develop and version a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow, then export as ProcessingStep

explanation: Data Wrangler flows allow interactive development of transformations, version control via Studio, and export as ProcessingStep for reproducible pipelines. Glue recipes aren’t integrated into pipelines, and Lambda lacks data science tooling.

stem: Your model inference is hosted using a Kubernetes-based mechanism requiring custom container orchestration. Which SageMaker deployment option allows you to maintain this while integrating with SageMaker Pipelines?

answers.A: SageMaker real-time endpoint with custom container
answers.B: Batch Transform job with custom transformer
answers.C: SageMaker serverless endpoint with custom container
answers.D: SageMaker Inference Realtime Inference on EKS

explanation: SageMaker Realtime Inference on EKS lets you deploy to your EKS cluster with custom orchestrations, integrating with pipelines. Standard endpoints and serverless endpoints abstract away Kubernetes.

stem: A compliance auditor requires a record of every data artifact and code version used in model training. Which combination ensures full traceability?

answers.A: S3 versioning + CloudTrail logs
answers.B: SageMaker Experiments lineage tracking + SageMaker Model Registry
answers.C: Git commit hashes in Glue ETL + DynamoDB audit table
answers.D: AWS Config recording S3 changes

explanation: Experiments track data and code versions at the run level, and Model Registry ties model artifacts to training runs, providing end-to-end ML lineage. S3 versioning and CloudTrail are lower-level and not ML-specific.

stem: Your application needs low-latency access to inference results but generates heavy batched requests. Which inference architecture balances throughput and latency?

answers.A: Provisioned real-time endpoint only
answers.B: Batch Transform only
answers.C: Mixed: use serverless real-time endpoint for spikes and Batch Transform for bulk
answers.D: SageMaker multi-model endpoint only

explanation: Combining serverless real-time endpoints for unpredictable spikes and Batch Transform for bulk processing optimizes cost and performance. Single methods either overprovision or increase latency.

stem: To minimize training cost, you want managed spot training with checkpointing. Which configuration achieves this in SageMaker?

answers.A: Set TrainingJobStrategy to ‘SpotSingleNode’
answers.B: Enable ‘ManagedSpotTraining’ and configure checkpoint S3 path
answers.C: Use Spot Instances in EC2 training cluster
answers.D: Run training on a serverless notebook with spot instances

explanation: ManagedSpotTraining in SageMaker automatically provisions spot instances and saves checkpoints to S3. The other options are either invalid or require manual orchestration outside SageMaker training jobs.

stem: Your ML pipeline must load features for offline training and serve the same features for online inference with single-digit millisecond latency. Which design meets these SLAs?

answers.A: Use SageMaker Feature Store with both offline and online stores
answers.B: Store features in Amazon RDS and query via Lambda
answers.C: Store parquet files in S3 and use Athena for queries
answers.D: Use DynamoDB for offline and S3 for online

explanation: SageMaker Feature Store provides an offline store for training and an online store optimized for low-latency reads. The other options either lack performance or separate stores.

stem: You have an imbalance in real-time inference traffic and want dynamic endpoint scaling without idle cost. Which SageMaker feature should you use?

answers.A: Provisioned instance fleet with Auto Scaling
answers.B: Serverless inference
answers.C: Multi-model endpoint with provisioned instances
answers.D: Batch transform with event triggers

explanation: Serverless inference scales automatically to zero when idle and scales with demand, avoiding idle costs. Auto Scaling of provisioned fleets still incurs minimum capacity costs.

stem: To enforce data schema and quality checks before training, you need a managed solution in your pipeline. Which SageMaker component should you integrate?

answers.A: SageMaker Clarify**BiasReportStep**
answers.B: Glue Data Catalog crawler
answers.C: Athena schema validation
answers.D: Model Monitor DataQualityJobDefinition

explanation: Model Monitor's DataQualityJobDefinition can be used in pipelines to validate data schema and detect anomalies before training. Clarify is for bias/fairness, and Glue/Athena are not ML-specific.

stem: A newly trained model shows lower inference accuracy in production than during testing. Which multi-step solution most directly addresses this?

answers.A: Increase instance size of endpoint and redeploy
answers.B: Retrain the model weekly with latest data
answers.C: Use Model Monitor to detect drift×trigger retraining pipeline
answers.D: Add more hidden layers to the neural network

explanation: The correct approach is to detect data drift with Model Monitor, then trigger automated retraining. Changing instance size or model architecture without addressing drift won't fix production accuracy declines.

stem: You need to run a hyperparameter tuning job and automatically compare results across multiple experiments and datasets. Which SageMaker features will you combine?

answers.A: SageMaker Hyperparameter TuningJob integrated with Experiments
answers.B: CloudWatch metrics filtered by TrainingJob name
answers.C: Athena queries on S3 logs
answers.D: Manual Excel aggregation of results

explanation: Hyperparameter TuningJobs integrated with SageMaker Experiments allow automated tracking and comparison of trials across experiments. CloudWatch and manual methods lack structured ML metadata.

stem: Which evaluation approach is most appropriate when your business objective values the top 10% of predictions being correct, regardless of overall recall?

answers.A: ROC AUC
answers.B: Overall accuracy
answers.C: F1-score
answers.D: Precision at N% (e.g., Precision@10%)

explanation: Precision@N% measures correctness within the top-scoring N% of predictions, aligning directly with business objectives. Other metrics don’t focus on a specific percentile cutoff.

stem: To version-control your pipeline definitions and allow pull requests for change management, which AWS service integration is recommended?

answers.A: Store pipeline JSON in S3 with versioning enabled
answers.B: Integrate SageMaker Studio with AWS CodeCommit
answers.C: Use DynamoDB to store pipeline definitions
answers.D: Embed pipeline definitions as Lambda code

explanation: SageMaker Studio can integrate with CodeCommit, allowing Git-based workflows for pipeline definitions. S3 versioning doesn’t provide pull requests and code review workflows.

stem: Your deployment requires A/B testing two model variants with 20% traffic on the new variant. Which SageMaker feature allows this traffic split?

answers.A: Provision two separate endpoints and use a Lambda router
answers.B: Use Batch Transform for variant testing
answers.C: Specify ProductionVariants with InitialVariantWeight in CreateEndpointConfig
answers.D: Deploy new variant to serverless endpoint

explanation: Setting InitialVariantWeight in a ProductionVariants array when creating an endpoint config splits traffic between variants. Other approaches are more complex and not built in.

stem: You want to integrate fairness and bias detection in your preprocessing and post-training steps within a SageMaker pipeline. Which components should you use in the respective steps?

answers.A: ClarifyDataQualityCheck for preprocessing and ClarifyBiasCheck for post-training
answers.B: ModelMonitor for preprocessing and Clarify for post-training
answers.C: Glue DataBrew recipe for both steps
answers.D: Athena queries for preprocessing and CloudWatch alarms for post-training

explanation: SageMaker Clarify’s data quality check can be used before training, and its bias check after training, within pipelines. Model Monitor focuses on drift and quality, not fairness.

stem: When using a subword tokenizer (like byte-pair encoding) for a generative AI foundation model, which scenario best explains a drawback of using a very small vocabulary size?

answers.A: Frequent words get split into many subwords, increasing sequence length and reducing generation efficiency.
answers.B: The model fails to represent rare words, leading to unknown token outputs for uncommon terms.
answers.C: A larger embedding matrix is required, increasing memory usage.
answers.D: It prevents the model from learning long-range dependencies due to positional errors.

explanation: A is correct because a small vocabulary forces common words into multiple subwords and lengthens context. B is wrong because subword tokenizers compose rare words from subwords. C is wrong since smaller vocab shrinks the embedding matrix. D is unrelated to vocabulary size.

stem: In a retrieval-augmented generation system, why is chunking long documents with overlapping windows often preferred over non-overlapping chunks?

answers.A: Overlapping windows improve continuity across boundaries to prevent missing context.
answers.B: They reduce total number of chunks, saving storage.
answers.C: They ensure equal token counts per chunk to meet fixed-size model input.
answers.D: They allow each chunk to be processed in parallel without context duplication.

explanation: A is correct because overlaps preserve context at boundaries. B is false—overlap increases chunk count. C is irrelevant to overlap. D is incorrect since overlap duplicates context, not eliminates it.

stem: A team must choose an embedding dimension for text vectors in a generative AI application. Which factor primarily influences selecting a higher dimensionality for embeddings?

answers.A: Larger vocabulary size and semantic granularity demand more dimensions to capture nuanced relationships.
answers.B: Increased batch size during training requires higher embedding dimensions for convergence.
answers.C: Lower model inference latency favors higher dimensions to speed similarity searches.
answers.D: The number of transformer layers directly scales with embedding dimension.

explanation: A is correct because richer semantics and more tokens require larger embeddings. B is unrelated to dimension. C is opposite—higher dimensions often slow similarity searches. D is false—layers and embedding size are independent choices.

stem: When comparing two text embeddings for semantic similarity, which metric is most appropriate to mitigate discrepancies in vector magnitude due to token count differences?

answers.A: Cosine similarity because it normalizes magnitude.
answers.B: Euclidean distance because it captures absolute distance.
answers.C: Dot product because it's faster on GPUs.
answers.D: Manhattan distance because it's robust to outliers.

explanation: A is correct since cosine similarity ignores vector length and focuses on angle. B and D use absolute distances influenced by magnitude. C’s speed claim ignores the normalization benefit of cosine.

stem: To improve reasoning in a generative AI model, a prompt engineer uses chain-of-thought prompts. What’s a potential drawback of this technique?

answers.A: It increases latency and token usage, possibly hitting context limits.
answers.B: It leads the model to ignore the final instruction and focus on intermediate steps.
answers.C: It reduces model creativity by constraining outputs.
answers.D: It causes the model to hallucinate numeric values more frequently.

explanation: A is correct because verbose reasoning consumes context and compute. B is incorrect—models still follow instructions. C and D are not established drawbacks tied specifically to chain-of-thought.

stem: In transformer-based generative AI, what is the purpose of using a causal attention mask during training?

answers.A: To prevent the model from attending to future tokens, enforcing autoregressive generation.
answers.B: To ensure the model attends equally to all tokens regardless of position.
answers.C: To reduce computational complexity by masking low-attention heads.
answers.D: To allow bidirectional context for improved semantic encoding.

explanation: A is correct—causal masks block future tokens. B, C, and D describe other mechanisms not achieved by causal masking.

stem: A company requires rapid prototyping with foundation models but limited compute. Which model-size tradeoff should they consider?

answers.A: Choosing a medium-sized model to balance latency and performance.
answers.B: Selecting the largest available model for higher accuracy despite slower inference.
answers.C: Using a tiny model as it guarantees zero hallucinations.
answers.D: Fine-tuning a very large model to reduce deployment cost.

explanation: A is correct—a medium model balances speed and quality. B ignores latency constraints. C is false—tiny models can still hallucinate. D increases cost, not reduces it.

stem: A generative AI application needs to caption images and also generate layouts. Why would a multi-modal foundation model be preferred over a unimodal text model?

answers.A: It natively processes visual features and textual patterns in a shared embedding space.
answers.B: It reduces the number of parameters compared to separate image and text models.
answers.C: It improves tokenization speed by merging pixels and text tokens.
answers.D: It avoids any need for positional embeddings for images.

explanation: A is correct—multi-modal models jointly embed images and text. B is wrong—multi-modal often adds parameters. C and D are incorrect technical claims.

stem: When fine-tuning a diffusion model for faster image synthesis, which modification to the noise schedule can accelerate generation without severely degrading quality?

answers.A: Reducing the number of denoising timesteps and adjusting the variance schedule to concentrate noise removal.
answers.B: Increasing the initial noise variance to cover broader solutions.
answers.C: Using a linear noise schedule instead of cosine to simplify computations.
answers.D: Removing the stochastic sampling step entirely to get deterministic outputs.

explanation: A is correct—fewer steps with tuned variance speeds up inference. B, C, and D either degrade quality severely or break the diffusion process.

stem: In a generative AI system employing vector quantization on embeddings, what is a primary disadvantage of aggressive quantization (e.g., fewer codebook entries)?

answers.A: Loss of semantic nuance leading to lower generation fidelity.
answers.B: Increased storage overhead from larger codebooks.
answers.C: Slower similarity searches due to coarse quantization.
answers.D: Higher risk of overfitting the quantized vectors.

explanation: A is correct—too few codebook entries degrade fidelity. B is opposite—fewer entries save storage. C is false—coarser quantization speeds search. D is unrelated.

stem: For RAG over a large PDF, what overlap ratio between chunks helps avoid context loss at chunk boundaries while minimizing redundancy?

answers.A: 10-20% overlap balances context carryover with storage.
answers.B: 50% overlap ensures no context is lost but doubles storage.
answers.C: 0% overlap maximizes chunk independence and reduces size.
answers.D: 80% overlap is needed to capture extended references across pages.

explanation: A is correct—small overlap preserves boundary context without excessive duplication. B and D waste storage; C loses context.

stem: A developer must choose between Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) and an IVF index in FAISS for embedding retrieval. Which scenario favors LSH?

answers.A: When memory is extremely limited and approximate retrieval is acceptable.
answers.B: When exact nearest neighbors are required for high-precision tasks.
answers.C: When embedding dimension exceeds GPU memory for IVF.
answers.D: When dynamic updates require fast insertion and deletion.

explanation: A is correct—LSH is lightweight and approximate. B demands exact search, favoring IVF or exact indices. C and D are unrelated trade-offs.

stem: What is a subtle prompt injection risk when concatenating user input with a system prompt in a generative AI chatbot?

answers.A: A user embeds instructions that override system directives, altering model behavior.
answers.B: The model increases hallucination rates due to longer inputs.
answers.C: The system prompt loses embedding effects due to position bias.
answers.D: The user’s input is truncated entirely during tokenization.

explanation: A is correct—malicious input can override system rules. B–D describe unrelated or less subtle issues.

stem: Compared to prefix-tuning a foundation model, what is a disadvantage of instruction fine-tuning?

answers.A: Instruction fine-tuning requires updating entire model weights, incurring higher compute cost.
answers.B: It cannot incorporate human feedback.
answers.C: It fails to improve performance on unseen tasks.
answers.D: It reduces the model’s context window.

explanation: A is correct—full fine-tuning is expensive. B–D are incorrect statements about instruction fine-tuning.

stem: Why might a byte-level BPE tokenizer yield better out-of-vocabulary handling than a word-level tokenizer in a multilingual generative model?

answers.A: It can break unknown words into known byte sequences, avoiding unknown tokens.
answers.B: It stores full words for all languages, increasing vocabulary.
answers.C: It reduces model perplexity uniformly across languages.
answers.D: It simplifies position embeddings by using bytes.

explanation: A is correct—byte-level BPE composes unknown words. B–D are incorrect or irrelevant advantages.

stem: A prompt engineer observes that lowering the temperature to 0.2 yields overly generic outputs. What’s causing this behavior?

answers.A: Low temperature sharpens the distribution, making the model choose high-probability tokens repeatedly.
answers.B: It increases sampling variance, leading to unpredictable results.
answers.C: It normalizes logits, causing underflow in softmax.
