Determining network configurations that can scale to accommodate future needs

stem: A company deploys a fleet of web servers that must be highly available across hardware failures but are in the same AZ for compliance reasons. What EC2 placement strategy should be used?

answers.A: Cluster placement group: places instances close together for low latency.
answers.B: Spread placement group: places each instance on distinct underlying hardware (rack), reducing the risk of simultaneous failure due to a single rack failure.
answers.C: Partition placement group: divides instances across logical partitions, each on different hardware.
answers.D: No placement group: EC2 distributes instances across hardware by default.

explanation: Spread placement groups place each instance on separate underlying hardware within the same AZ. A single hardware failure (rack, power, network) affects at most one instance. This provides maximum fault isolation within an AZ with a maximum of 7 instances per AZ per group. Cluster placement (A) optimises performance, not fault isolation. Partition placement (C) is designed for distributed systems like Hadoop/HDFS with groups of instances. Default placement (D) provides no hardware isolation guarantees.
tags: Selecting the appropriate load balancing strategy
Determining the appropriate placement of resources to meet business requirements

stem: A company runs a three-tier application: web servers in public subnets, application servers in private subnets, and RDS in isolated subnets. They want to add an ElastiCache Redis cluster for session caching. Where should the Redis cluster be placed?

answers.A: In public subnets so all application layers can reach it.
answers.B: In private subnets, co-located with the application servers; Redis is accessed only by application servers and should not be internet-accessible.
answers.C: In isolated subnets with the RDS database to consolidate backend resources.
answers.D: In a separate VPC peered to the application VPC.

explanation: ElastiCache should be in private subnets accessible only to the application tier. Redis should never be internet-accessible (it lacks strong authentication by default). Placing it in private subnets with security groups allowing inbound from application server security groups is the correct design. Public subnets (A) expose Redis to the internet. Isolated subnets with RDS (C) may restrict Redis from being reachable by app servers. A separate VPC (D) adds unnecessary complexity.

stem: A company has three services: (1) a user-facing HTTPS web app that routes based on URL path, (2) a high-throughput UDP game server, and (3) a third-party virtual network appliance for packet inspection. Which load balancer type should be used for each?

answers.A: ALB for all three services.
answers.B: ALB for the HTTPS web app (path-based routing); NLB for the UDP game server (Layer 4, UDP support); GLB for the packet inspection appliance (transparent bump-in-the-wire).
answers.C: NLB for all three: handles all protocols and provides lowest latency.
answers.D: CLB for HTTPS, NLB for UDP, and ALB for packet inspection.

explanation: ALB (Layer 7) supports content-based routing (path, host, headers) for HTTP/HTTPS. NLB (Layer 4) supports TCP, UDP, and TLS with ultra-high throughput and static IPs. Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) is purpose-built for third-party network appliance integration with transparent traffic routing. ALBs do not support UDP. NLBs don't support path-based routing. GLBs are not used for application traffic — they're for inline appliance insertion.

stem: A company migrates an existing application behind a Classic Load Balancer (CLB) to a modern load balancer. The application uses HTTP/2, requires path-based routing across 5 microservices, and must support gRPC. Which load balancer replacement is most appropriate?

answers.A: Network Load Balancer: supports all protocols with the lowest latency.
answers.B: Application Load Balancer: supports HTTP/2, gRPC, and path-based routing rules with multiple target groups.
answers.C: Gateway Load Balancer: designed for transparent application routing.
answers.D: Classic Load Balancer with updated listeners for HTTP/2.

explanation: ALB supports HTTP/2, gRPC, and path-based routing to multiple target groups (one per microservice). It is the direct upgrade path from CLB for HTTP/HTTPS workloads. NLB (A) operates at Layer 4 and doesn't support path-based routing or gRPC at the application layer. GWLB (C) is for inline appliance inspection. CLB (D) does not support HTTP/2 or path-based routing — that's why a migration is needed.

stem: A VPC has a public subnet and a private subnet. The private subnet's route table has no route to an internet gateway. An EC2 instance in the private subnet needs to download software packages from the internet. Which solution is correct?

answers.A: Add a route 0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway in the private subnet route table.
answers.B: Deploy a NAT Gateway in the public subnet, add a route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway in the private subnet route table.
answers.C: Deploy a NAT Gateway in the private subnet, add a route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway in the private subnet route table.
answers.D: Enable DNS hostnames on the VPC so the private instance can resolve and reach internet addresses.

explanation: A NAT Gateway must reside in a public subnet (which has a direct route to the IGW). The private subnet route table then has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the NAT Gateway. This allows outbound-only internet access for private instances. Placing the NAT Gateway in the private subnet (C) is invalid — it needs a public subnet to relay traffic. Adding an IGW route to the private subnet (A) makes it a public subnet and exposes the instance directly. DNS hostnames (D) enable DNS resolution but don't provide routing.
tags: Identifying metrics based on business requirements to deliver a highly available solution

stem: A company has two VPCs peered together. VPC-A (10.0.0.0/16) and VPC-B (172.16.0.0/16). An instance in VPC-A cannot reach an instance in VPC-B despite the peering connection being active. What is the most likely cause?

answers.A: VPC peering does not support cross-VPC communication between instances.
answers.B: The route tables in both VPCs are missing entries for the peer CIDR ranges pointing to the peering connection.
answers.C: Security groups in both VPCs allow all traffic by default, so the issue is with NACLs blocking traffic.
answers.D: The VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges, which prevents route table entries from being added.

explanation: A VPC peering connection alone does not route traffic. Route table entries must be manually added in both VPCs: VPC-A needs a route for 172.16.0.0/16 → pcx-xxx, and VPC-B needs a route for 10.0.0.0/16 → pcx-xxx. Security groups also need to allow traffic, but the most common and likely cause of no connectivity with an active peering connection is missing route table entries.
tags: Using AWS services that improve the reliability of legacy applications and applications not built for the cloud (for example, when application changes are not possible)
AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)

stem: A serverless application using hundreds of Lambda functions connects directly to an RDS PostgreSQL database. During traffic spikes, the database reports 'too many connections' errors and performance degrades. Which solution best addresses this with minimal application changes?

answers.A: Increase the max_connections parameter on the RDS instance.
answers.B: Add RDS Proxy between Lambda and RDS; configure the Lambda functions to connect via the proxy endpoint.
answers.C: Switch from RDS PostgreSQL to DynamoDB, which has no connection limits.
answers.D: Reduce Lambda concurrency to limit the number of simultaneous database connections.

explanation: RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool to RDS and multiplexes thousands of Lambda connections into a small number of persistent database connections. Lambda's function-per-request model creates a new connection for each invocation, which exhausts database connection limits. RDS Proxy is purpose-built for serverless workloads and requires only a connection string change. Increasing max_connections (A) has limits and doesn't solve pooling. DynamoDB (C) requires significant application refactoring. Reducing concurrency (D) throttles the application rather than solving the root cause.
tags: Using purpose-built AWS services for workloads
Proxy concepts (for example, Amazon RDS Proxy)

stem: An RDS Multi-AZ instance has RDS Proxy configured in front of it. During a database failover, what is the benefit of using RDS Proxy for the application?

answers.A: RDS Proxy prevents failover entirely by keeping the primary instance alive.
answers.B: RDS Proxy reduces failover time visible to the application by maintaining connections and re-routing them to the new primary with minimal disruption, reducing failover impact from minutes to seconds.
answers.C: RDS Proxy caches all database responses so the application continues to read data during the failover without any latency.
answers.D: RDS Proxy replicates writes to both the primary and standby, eliminating data loss during failover.

explanation: During an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the DNS endpoint switches to the standby (typically 60-120 seconds). With RDS Proxy, the application connects to the proxy endpoint (which does not change). The proxy detects the failover and pins connections to the new primary, reducing the application-visible disruption from 60-120 seconds to a few seconds. The proxy does not prevent failover, cache all responses, or replicate writes.
tags: Proxy concepts (for example, Amazon RDS Proxy)

stem: A company needs to store large video files (each 50 GB) that are uploaded once, accessed frequently for the first 30 days, then rarely accessed. They require 11 nines of durability. Which S3 storage class progression achieves the lowest cost?

answers.A: S3 Standard → S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval via lifecycle policy at 30 days.
answers.B: S3 Standard → S3 Standard-IA via lifecycle policy at 30 days.
answers.C: S3 Reduced Redundancy Storage for all objects.
answers.D: S3 One Zone-IA for all objects to minimize cost.

explanation: S3 Standard provides frequent-access performance and 11 nines of durability. After 30 days, S3 Standard-IA provides the same 11 nines of durability at ~60% lower storage cost with a per-retrieval fee — appropriate for infrequent access. Glacier (A) has retrieval delays (minutes to hours) unsuitable for 'rarely but still accessed' media. Reduced Redundancy (C) provides only 4 nines of durability, violating the requirement. S3 One Zone-IA (D) stores data in one AZ with only 11 nines of durability within that AZ, risking data loss if the AZ fails.
tags: Implementing strategies to ensure the durability and availability of data (for example, backups)
Storage options and characteristics (for example, durability, replication)

stem: A company uses Amazon EFS for shared file storage across EC2 instances in multiple AZs. They need to understand the durability characteristics of EFS. Which statement is correct?

answers.A: EFS stores data in a single AZ with 11 nines of durability.
answers.B: EFS stores data redundantly across multiple AZs within a region, providing 11 nines of durability.
answers.C: EFS stores data on instance-attached NVMe drives, providing high durability through RAID-1 mirroring.
answers.D: EFS durability is equivalent to EBS gp2 volumes: 99.8-99.9%.

explanation: Amazon EFS (Standard storage class) stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones within an AWS Region, providing 11 nines (99.999999999%) of durability. This multi-AZ replication is automatic. EFS One Zone is the exception — it stores data in a single AZ. EFS does not use instance NVMe drives; it's a managed network file system. EBS gp2 durability figures apply to block storage, not EFS.

stem: A company wants to query data stored in S3 in Parquet format without loading it into a database. Results must be available within seconds for ad-hoc queries. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon Redshift: load Parquet files into Redshift tables then query with SQL.
answers.B: Amazon Athena: serverless SQL query engine that queries Parquet files in S3 directly, with no infrastructure to manage.
answers.C: Amazon EMR with Apache Spark: run distributed Spark SQL queries against S3 Parquet files.
answers.D: AWS Glue ETL: transform Parquet files to CSV then load into RDS for querying.

explanation: Amazon Athena is purpose-built for serverless, ad-hoc SQL queries directly against S3. It supports Parquet natively and charges per TB scanned. No infrastructure provisioning is required and queries return in seconds. Redshift (A) requires loading data and cluster management. EMR (C) requires cluster provisioning and is more appropriate for large-scale transformation jobs, not quick ad-hoc queries. Glue ETL (D) is a transformation service, not a query service.

stem: A data team needs to create interactive dashboards and visualizations from their Redshift data warehouse for business stakeholders who have no SQL skills. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon Athena: allows stakeholders to run SQL queries against S3.
answers.B: Amazon QuickSight: fully managed BI service with drag-and-drop dashboard creation, ML-powered insights, and direct Redshift connectivity.
answers.C: AWS Glue DataBrew: no-code data transformation and profiling tool.
answers.D: Amazon SageMaker Studio: ML-focused notebooks for data exploration.

explanation: Amazon QuickSight is AWS's managed Business Intelligence (BI) service designed for non-technical users to create interactive dashboards, visualizations, and reports. It connects natively to Redshift, S3, Athena, and other sources. QuickSight's SPICE engine accelerates queries. Athena (A) requires SQL knowledge. DataBrew (C) is for data preparation and profiling. SageMaker Studio (D) is for ML practitioners, not business stakeholders creating dashboards.

stem: A company needs to build a data lake on S3 with centralized access controls, data cataloguing, and column-level security for sensitive PII data. Which AWS service provides these capabilities?

answers.A: AWS Glue Data Catalog alone: provides a metadata catalog but no access control features.
answers.B: AWS Lake Formation: provides centralized data lake governance, fine-grained (database, table, column, row) access controls on top of the Glue Data Catalog, and integrates with Athena and Redshift.
answers.C: Amazon Macie: provides PII detection and S3 security configuration.
answers.D: AWS IAM: manage S3 bucket policies for column-level access to Parquet files.

explanation: AWS Lake Formation provides centralized governance for data lakes. It extends the Glue Data Catalog with fine-grained access control down to column and row level. Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and other services enforce Lake Formation permissions when querying data. Glue Data Catalog (A) provides metadata but not fine-grained access control. Macie (C) detects PII but doesn't enforce column-level access. S3 IAM policies (D) operate at the object level, not column level.
tags: Data transfer services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Storage Gateway)

stem: A retail company needs to load daily sales transaction files from on-premises systems into an S3 data lake at midnight each night. The files are up to 500 GB. Which ingestion approach is most operationally simple?

answers.A: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams: stream each transaction as it occurs throughout the day.
answers.B: AWS DataSync scheduled transfer: schedule a nightly DataSync task to copy files from on-premises NFS to S3.
answers.C: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation: buffer records and deliver to S3 every hour.
answers.D: Set up an AWS Direct Connect dedicated line and manually scp files using a cron job.

explanation: AWS DataSync is designed for scheduled, large-scale file transfers from on-premises NFS/SMB to S3 (or EFS, FSx). It handles scheduling, encryption in transit, data integrity validation, and bandwidth throttling. For batch/nightly loads, DataSync is operationally simpler than streaming services. Kinesis Data Streams (A) and Firehose (C) are for continuous real-time streaming, not nightly batch file transfers. Manual scp (D) requires infrastructure management and lacks reliability features.
tags: Streaming data services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Kinesis)

stem: A company ingests social media event data that arrives continuously at ~10,000 events per second. They need near-real-time processing and delivery to S3 in Parquet format. Which ingestion service is most suitable?

answers.A: AWS Batch: process events on a scheduled batch cycle.
answers.B: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose: buffers streaming records, optionally transforms via Lambda (to Parquet), and delivers to S3 with configurable buffering intervals.
answers.C: AWS Glue ETL job: triggered hourly to process accumulated records from an SQS queue.
answers.D: AWS Transfer Family SFTP: accepts files from the social media API.

explanation: Kinesis Data Firehose handles high-throughput continuous streaming data. It buffers records and can invoke Lambda to convert JSON to Parquet before writing to S3. It requires no infrastructure management. AWS Batch (A) is for batch jobs, not continuous streaming. Glue ETL (C) has startup overhead and is not suitable for near-real-time. Transfer Family (D) is for managed file transfers (SFTP/FTP), not API event streams.

stem: A company uses Kinesis Data Streams to ingest sensitive financial data from EC2 instances in a private VPC subnet. They must ensure the data never traverses the public internet. Which configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Enable HTTPS on the Kinesis SDK — data is encrypted in transit and never crosses the public internet.
answers.B: Create a VPC endpoint (Interface endpoint) for Kinesis Data Streams in the VPC, update the route table, and configure the producer to use the VPC endpoint DNS name.
answers.C: Configure the Kinesis stream with a resource-based policy allowing only the VPC's IP range.
answers.D: Deploy the EC2 producers in a public subnet so they can reach the Kinesis public endpoint directly.

explanation: A VPC Interface Endpoint for Kinesis Data Streams creates a private connection from the VPC to Kinesis using AWS PrivateLink, keeping traffic entirely within the AWS network. HTTPS (A) encrypts data in transit but still routes over the public internet. A resource-based policy restricting to a VPC IP range (C) does not prevent internet routing — it only restricts which sources can call the API. Moving producers to a public subnet (D) exposes them and uses the public internet.

stem: An organization uses Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver data to an S3 bucket. They need to ensure only the Firehose delivery stream can write to the S3 bucket. Which combination of controls achieves this?

answers.A: Enable S3 Block Public Access and use default encryption.
answers.B: Attach an S3 bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject only from the Firehose IAM service role ARN, and attach an IAM role to Firehose with s3:PutObject on the target bucket.
answers.C: Enable S3 Object Lock to prevent writes from unauthorized sources.
answers.D: Use S3 Access Points to limit the Firehose delivery to a specific prefix.

explanation: The correct pattern is dual-sided: (1) the Firehose delivery stream assumes an IAM role with s3:PutObject permissions on the target bucket, and (2) the S3 bucket policy restricts writes using aws:PrincipalArn to only that IAM role. This ensures only the Firehose role can write. Block Public Access (A) prevents public access but doesn't restrict which AWS principals can write. Object Lock (C) prevents deletion/overwrite of objects but doesn't restrict who can create new objects. Access Points (D) provide an alternative access path but don't inherently restrict writes to Firehose.
tags: Secure access to ingestion access points

stem: A company is migrating 500 TB of archival data from on-premises to S3. Their internet connection is 100 Mbps shared with business operations. At 80% utilization, the transfer would take over 600 days. Which AWS service solves this?

answers.A: Increase the internet bandwidth to 10 Gbps to reduce transfer time.
answers.B: Use AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices: ship data to AWS on physical appliances for ingestion into S3, bypassing the internet connection.
answers.C: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration to boost upload speeds over the existing 100 Mbps link.
answers.D: Use AWS DataSync to optimize and accelerate the 100 Mbps connection with compression.

explanation: AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized transfers data physically. A single Snowball Edge holds 80 TB, so roughly 7 devices cover 500 TB, and data can be transferred in days (shipping time) rather than 600+ days. S3 Transfer Acceleration (C) improves internet transfer speeds using CloudFront edge nodes but is still bounded by the 100 Mbps link. DataSync (D) compresses data but cannot overcome a fundamentally insufficient bandwidth. Upgrading internet bandwidth (A) is costly and still slower than physical transfer.
tags: Data transfer services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Storage Gateway)

stem: A media company needs to transfer 10 TB of new 4K video files from an on-premises NAS to S3 every day. Their 1 Gbps internet link is used at 50% by normal operations. How much bandwidth is available for transfers, and which AWS service is most appropriate for this sustained daily transfer?

answers.A: Available: 500 Mbps. Use S3 multipart upload with the AWS CLI directly from the NAS.
answers.B: Available: 500 Mbps. Use AWS DataSync with bandwidth throttling to manage co-existence with business traffic.
answers.C: Available: 500 Mbps. Use AWS Snowball to ship drives weekly.
answers.D: Available: 1 Gbps. Use AWS Direct Connect dedicated to media transfers.

explanation: With 50% utilization, 500 Mbps is available. At 500 Mbps, 10 TB transfers in approximately 44 minutes — well within a 24-hour window. AWS DataSync is optimized for large file transfers from NAS (NFS/SMB) to S3, supports bandwidth throttling (to coexist with business traffic), verifies data integrity, and handles the operational complexity of daily transfers. Plain multipart upload (A) requires custom scripting and no throttling. Snowball (C) is for one-off or very large migrations, not daily recurring 10 TB transfers. Direct Connect (D) is appropriate for very high sustained throughput but is more expensive and complex.
tags: Data transfer services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Storage Gateway)

stem: A company builds a data lake on S3 with multiple teams needing access to different subsets of data. Some tables contain sensitive PII columns that must be hidden from most users. Which architecture achieves fine-grained access control?

answers.A: Create separate S3 buckets per team with individual bucket policies — each team can only access their bucket.
answers.B: Use AWS Lake Formation to register the S3 location, define the data catalog in AWS Glue, and grant column-level and row-level permissions to IAM roles/groups through Lake Formation.
answers.C: Enable S3 Object-level logging with CloudTrail and block unauthorized access via Lambda-triggered access denials.
answers.D: Use Amazon Macie to automatically hide PII columns from non-privileged users.

explanation: Lake Formation provides the only native AWS mechanism for column-level and row-level security on data lake tables. It integrates with the Glue Data Catalog and enforces permissions when data is queried through Athena, Redshift Spectrum, or EMR. Separate buckets (A) work for coarse-grained separation but don't support column-level control. CloudTrail/Lambda (C) can audit but not prevent access in real time at the column level. Macie (D) detects PII but does not enforce access restrictions.

stem: A company's S3 data lake receives raw data from multiple sources. They need to catalog all datasets automatically so analysts can discover available data, and they need to track schema changes over time. Which AWS service combination achieves this?

answers.A: Amazon Athena: creates tables from S3 data on demand when analysts run queries.
answers.B: AWS Glue Crawler: automatically crawls S3 locations on a schedule, infers schemas, and populates the Glue Data Catalog with table definitions including schema versioning.
answers.C: Amazon S3 Inventory: generates weekly reports of all objects in a bucket with metadata.
answers.D: AWS Config: tracks S3 bucket configuration changes and schema drift.

explanation: AWS Glue Crawlers automatically discover data formats (CSV, Parquet, JSON, Avro), infer schemas, and create/update table definitions in the Glue Data Catalog. They track schema changes by creating new schema versions. The Data Catalog makes datasets discoverable for Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR. Athena (A) creates tables on demand but doesn't auto-discover or track schema changes. S3 Inventory (C) lists objects and metadata but doesn't infer data schemas. AWS Config (D) tracks infrastructure configuration, not data schemas.
tags: Transforming data between formats (for example, .csv to .parquet)

stem: A company needs to process clickstream events from a web application at 50,000 events/second. The events must be analyzed in real time for fraud detection and also stored in S3 for historical analysis. Which architecture is most appropriate?

answers.A: Write events to RDS, run fraud detection queries with SQL, and export results to S3 nightly.
answers.B: Ingest events into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams; have a Kinesis Data Analytics (Apache Flink) application read from the stream for real-time fraud detection; simultaneously use Kinesis Data Firehose to buffer and deliver events to S3.
answers.C: Ingest events to SQS FIFO queue; process with Lambda for fraud detection; export from SQS to S3 daily.
answers.D: Ingest events to Amazon MSK (Kafka); use EC2-hosted Spark Streaming for fraud detection; write to S3 via EMR.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams handles 50,000 events/second at scale. Kinesis Data Analytics (Flink) provides sub-second real-time processing for fraud detection with SQL/Flink APIs. Firehose is a separate consumer that buffers and delivers to S3 cost-effectively. This fan-out pattern (one stream, multiple consumers) is the canonical AWS real-time + archive pattern. RDS (A) cannot handle 50K events/second for writes. SQS FIFO (C) has 300 msg/s limit per queue. MSK+EMR (D) works but requires significant infrastructure management.
tags: Data analytics and visualization services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Athena, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon QuickSuite)
Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)

stem: A company wants to build a data pipeline that reads from an Amazon MSK (Kafka) topic, transforms records using Apache Flink (filtering PII, enriching with reference data), and delivers to both Amazon S3 and Amazon OpenSearch Service for search. Which AWS managed service handles the Flink processing?

answers.A: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams: re-ingest MSK records into Kinesis for Flink processing.
answers.B: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics): runs managed Flink applications that read from MSK, process records, and write to multiple sinks including S3 and OpenSearch.
answers.C: AWS Lambda: invoke from MSK trigger, process records, and write to S3 and OpenSearch.
answers.D: Amazon EMR with Apache Flink installed: launch a cluster, configure MSK connector, and run Flink jobs.

explanation: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (MSF) is the fully managed Flink service that reads from MSK (Kafka) natively, runs stateful stream processing (filtering, enrichment, joins), and writes to multiple sinks (S3, OpenSearch, Kinesis, etc.). No cluster management is required. Kinesis Data Streams (A) is a different streaming service and doesn't re-ingest from MSK. Lambda (C) has a 15-minute timeout and is not suited for stateful streaming joins or complex transformations. EMR Flink (D) requires cluster provisioning, scaling, and lifecycle management.
tags: Streaming data services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Kinesis)
Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK)

stem: A company continuously syncs data between two S3 buckets in different AWS regions for compliance reasons. They need bidirectional replication with low latency and the ability to handle conflicts. Which S3 feature achieves this?

answers.A: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) configured in both directions with a Lambda function to detect and resolve conflicts.
answers.B: S3 Multi-Region Access Points with S3 Replication: configure two-way replication rules between the buckets.
answers.C: S3 Batch Operations: run a daily job to sync objects between regions.
answers.D: AWS DataSync scheduled task running every 5 minutes to sync both buckets bidirectionally.

explanation: S3 Multi-Region Access Points with bidirectional replication rules support two-way replication between S3 buckets. S3 Replication includes conflict resolution (last-writer-wins based on replication time). One-way CRR (A) with Lambda conflict detection requires custom development and adds latency. S3 Batch Operations (C) are for bulk operations, not continuous sync. DataSync (D) is for on-premises-to-cloud or EFS/FSx transfers, not optimal for S3-to-S3 continuous replication.
tags: Secure access to ingestion access points

stem: A business intelligence team wants to share interactive dashboards with 500 external partners who should not need to create AWS accounts. The dashboards use Amazon QuickSight. Which QuickSight capability supports this?

answers.A: QuickSight Standard edition: share dashboards via email links to external users with AWS accounts.
answers.B: QuickSight Embedded Analytics: embed dashboards in a partner portal using anonymous embedding or registered user embedding, without requiring AWS accounts.
answers.C: Amazon Managed Grafana: embed Grafana dashboards in an external portal.
answers.D: Create static PDF exports of QuickSight dashboards and email them to partners.

explanation: QuickSight Embedded Analytics allows dashboards to be embedded in external web applications. With anonymous embedding, end users don't need AWS accounts or QuickSight subscriptions; they access dashboards through the host application. This is the correct solution for external partners. Standard sharing (A) requires users to have QuickSight accounts. Grafana (C) is a separate product not tied to QuickSight. Static PDF exports (D) are not interactive.
tags: Secure access to ingestion access points
Sizes and speeds needed to meet business requirements

stem: A data team uses Amazon Athena to query S3 data and Amazon QuickSight to visualize results. Analysts report dashboard load times of 30-60 seconds. Which QuickSight feature most effectively reduces this to under 5 seconds?

answers.A: Switch from Athena to Redshift as the QuickSight data source.
answers.B: Enable SPICE (Super-fast Parallel In-memory Calculation Engine): import the Athena query results into SPICE, which serves queries from in-memory at sub-second speed.
answers.C: Use QuickSight ML Insights to pre-compute dashboard results.
answers.D: Increase the Athena query result cache TTL to 24 hours.

explanation: SPICE is QuickSight's in-memory calculation engine. When data is imported into SPICE, dashboard queries are served from memory rather than running live Athena queries against S3, reducing load times from seconds/minutes to milliseconds. SPICE is refreshed on a schedule to keep data current. Switching to Redshift (A) may improve Athena query speeds but still involves live database queries. ML Insights (C) provides anomaly detection and forecasting, not general query acceleration. Athena's result cache (D) helps with repeated identical queries but doesn't accelerate varied dashboard interactions.

stem: A data engineering team runs Apache Spark jobs that process 50 TB of data daily. Jobs run for 2-4 hours, then the cluster sits idle. They want to reduce costs while maintaining performance. Which EMR configuration is most cost-effective?

answers.A: Use On-Demand instances only for all node types to ensure reliability.
answers.B: Use On-Demand for the master node, Reserved Instances for core nodes, and Spot Instances for task nodes — terminate the cluster after each job completes.
answers.C: Use Spot Instances for all node types including master.
answers.D: Use a persistent EMR cluster running 24/7 with Reserved Instances.

explanation: For transient EMR clusters: the master node should be On-Demand (terminating the master ends the job). Core nodes should be On-Demand or Reserved (they store HDFS data; Spot interruption loses data). Task nodes are ideal for Spot Instances — they process data but don't store HDFS data, so interruption only causes task retry without data loss. Terminating the cluster after each job eliminates idle compute cost. All-Spot master (C) risks data loss. 24/7 Reserved (D) wastes money during idle periods.
tags: Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)

stem: A company needs to run a one-time data transformation job on 10 TB of data stored in S3. The job transforms CSV to Parquet with schema normalization. They want the lowest operational overhead. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: Amazon EMR with a manually configured Apache Spark cluster.
answers.B: AWS Glue ETL job: serverless, pay-per-DPU-second, transforms S3 CSV data to Parquet with auto-generated or custom PySpark/Scala scripts.
answers.C: Amazon Athena CTAS (Create Table As Select): write Parquet output to S3 with a single SQL statement.
answers.D: AWS Lambda: process CSV records row by row and write Parquet output.

explanation: AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service with no cluster management. For a one-time transformation job, Glue provides auto-scaling workers (DPUs), built-in CSV-to-Parquet conversion, and you pay only for DPU-seconds used. EMR (A) requires cluster configuration, sizing, and management. Athena CTAS (C) can convert formats, but Glue handles larger volumes with more transformation complexity. Lambda (D) has a 15-minute timeout and 10 GB memory limit — too small for 10 TB without complex orchestration.
tags: Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)
Transforming data between formats (for example, .csv to .parquet)

stem: A company configures Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver streaming data to S3. They observe many small files (< 1 MB) being written to S3, which causes slow Athena query performance. Which Firehose configuration adjustment addresses this?

answers.A: Increase the Firehose shard count to write larger batches.
answers.B: Increase the Firehose buffering interval (e.g., to 900 seconds / 15 minutes) and the buffering size (e.g., 128 MB) so that Firehose accumulates more records before writing each S3 object.
answers.C: Enable Firehose data transformation with Lambda to merge small records into larger objects.
answers.D: Switch from S3 to Redshift as the Firehose destination to avoid the small-files problem.

explanation: Kinesis Data Firehose buffers records before writing to S3, with configurable interval (60-900 seconds) and size (1-128 MB) thresholds — it flushes whichever is hit first. Increasing both thresholds reduces file count and increases file size, which dramatically improves Athena query performance (Athena benefits from fewer, larger files). Firehose does not have 'shards' (that's Kinesis Data Streams). Lambda transformation (C) processes records but doesn't control output file size — that's the buffering configuration. Switching to Redshift (D) avoids S3 but doesn't solve the architectural question of small files.
tags: Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)

stem: A company ingests IoT sensor data using Kinesis Data Streams with 10 shards. Data producers sometimes generate duplicate records due to retry logic. Downstream consumers must process each record exactly once. Which approach addresses this?

answers.A: Enable Kinesis Enhanced Fan-Out to deduplicate records automatically.
answers.B: Use sequence numbers and shard IDs provided in each Kinesis record to implement idempotent processing; track already-processed sequence numbers in DynamoDB and skip duplicates.
answers.C: Enable Kinesis Data Streams server-side deduplication by setting DeduplicationEnabled=true.
answers.D: Increase shard count to 100 to distribute duplicates across more shards.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams does not provide built-in exactly-once delivery — it provides at-least-once semantics. To achieve exactly-once processing, consumers must implement idempotency: use the sequence number and shard ID as a unique key, store processed sequence numbers in DynamoDB, and skip records already processed. Enhanced Fan-Out (A) enables multiple consumers with dedicated throughput but doesn't deduplicate. There is no DeduplicationEnabled parameter in Kinesis (C). Adding shards (D) affects throughput, not deduplication.
tags: Selecting appropriate compute options for data processing (for example, Amazon EMR)

stem: A company hosts a public genomics dataset in S3 that is downloaded millions of times per day by external researchers. The company pays significant S3 data transfer costs. Which S3 feature shifts those costs to the researchers?

answers.A: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to reduce costs by routing through CloudFront.
answers.B: Enable the S3 Requester Pays feature on the bucket: requesters pay for data transfer and request costs, not the bucket owner.
answers.C: Create a CloudFront distribution in front of S3 to reduce origin data transfer charges.
answers.D: Move the dataset to S3 Glacier to reduce storage and transfer costs.

explanation: S3 Requester Pays transfers the cost of requests and data transfer from the bucket owner to the requesters. Requesters must authenticate with AWS credentials (anonymous access is disabled when Requester Pays is enabled). This is the purpose-built feature for sharing large public datasets where the provider should not bear transfer costs. CloudFront (C) reduces origin transfer costs using edge caching but the company still pays for distribution costs. Glacier (D) adds retrieval time and cost. Transfer Acceleration (A) speeds up uploads but doesn't shift costs.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

stem: A company has 50 teams using shared AWS accounts. The finance team needs to allocate S3, EC2, and RDS costs to individual teams in monthly cost reports. Which approach achieves this?

answers.A: Create separate AWS accounts per team — costs are naturally isolated.
answers.B: Define and enforce resource tagging with team identifiers (e.g., Team=Engineering); activate the tag as a cost allocation tag in Billing; use Cost Explorer filtered by the tag to produce per-team cost reports.
answers.C: Use AWS Budgets per service (S3, EC2, RDS) to alert when spending exceeds thresholds.
answers.D: Enable AWS Trusted Advisor to analyze per-team resource utilization.

explanation: Cost allocation tags are the standard mechanism for attributing shared-account costs to teams. Once a tag (e.g., Team=Engineering) is activated as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console, it appears as a filterable dimension in Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports (CUR). Separate accounts (A) provide the cleanest isolation but require significant account vending infrastructure and don't apply retroactively. Budgets (C) alert on spending but don't allocate costs. Trusted Advisor (D) provides optimization recommendations, not cost attribution.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

stem: A large enterprise with 200 AWS accounts in an AWS Organization wants consolidated billing and volume pricing discounts. Which feature enables this?

answers.A: Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection in each account individually.
answers.B: Enable Consolidated Billing in AWS Organizations: all member account charges are combined in the management account bill, and volume tiered pricing (e.g., S3, data transfer) is calculated across all accounts.
answers.C: Use AWS Budgets in the management account to apply discount thresholds across member accounts.
answers.D: Purchase Reserved Instances in each account separately to maximize per-account discounts.

explanation: Consolidated Billing in AWS Organizations aggregates usage across all member accounts into a single bill in the management account. Volume pricing tiers (for services like S3, data transfer, and CloudFront) are calculated on the combined usage, resulting in lower per-unit costs. Reserved Instance and Savings Plans benefits are also shared across the organization. Cost Anomaly Detection (A) is per-account by default. Budgets (C) provide cost control alerts. Purchasing RIs separately (D) misses the shared RI benefit across accounts.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

stem: A company's AWS spending increased by 40% last month. The finance team needs to identify which service and region drove the increase and forecast next month's spend. Which tool is most appropriate?

answers.A: AWS Trusted Advisor: reviews resource utilization and provides cost savings recommendations.
answers.B: AWS Cost Explorer: provides interactive cost and usage graphs filterable by service, region, account, and tag, with 12-month historical data and 12-month forecasting.
answers.C: AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR): provides line-item granularity in S3 for custom analysis in Athena.
answers.D: AWS Budgets: sets spending thresholds and sends alerts when exceeded.

explanation: Cost Explorer is the interactive cost analysis and forecasting tool. It allows filtering by service, region, account, tag, purchase option, and more, with monthly and daily granularity. It also provides 12-month forecasts based on historical trends. CUR (C) provides the raw data for custom analysis but requires Athena/QuickSight setup — not immediately actionable for ad-hoc investigation. Trusted Advisor (A) gives optimization recommendations. Budgets (D) alerts on future spending but doesn't explain past increases.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)
AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

stem: A company wants to receive automated alerts when their total AWS spend is forecasted to exceed $10,000 in a month, not just when it has already exceeded the threshold. Which AWS service and configuration achieves this?

answers.A: AWS Cost Explorer forecast view: check daily and configure email reminders manually.
answers.B: AWS Budgets with a forecasted spend alert: set the budget amount to $10,000 and configure a forecasted threshold alert at 100% — Budgets will notify when the month-end forecast exceeds the budget before it happens.
answers.C: AWS CloudWatch: create a billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric with a threshold of $10,000.
answers.D: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: detects unexpected cost increases and alerts automatically.

explanation: AWS Budgets supports both actual spend alerts (already spent) and forecasted spend alerts (predicted to exceed by month-end) based on the forecasting model. This proactive alerting is distinct from CloudWatch billing alarms which only trigger on actual charges. CloudWatch billing alarms (C) alert when charges have already exceeded the threshold. Cost Explorer (A) requires manual checking. Cost Anomaly Detection (D) detects anomalies, not absolute budget thresholds.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)
AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

stem: A company runs a throughput-intensive big data processing workload that reads and writes large sequential files. The workload requires 500 MB/s throughput at the lowest cost. Which EBS volume type is most cost-effective?

answers.A: io2 Block Express: highest IOPS, but expensive for this workload.
answers.B: gp3: balanced SSD with configurable IOPS/throughput, max 1,000 MB/s.
answers.C: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD): designed for large sequential workloads with up to 500 MB/s at significantly lower cost than SSD.
answers.D: sc1 (Cold HDD): lowest cost HDD, but limited to 250 MB/s throughput.

explanation: st1 is purpose-built for throughput-intensive sequential workloads (log processing, big data, data warehouses) and provides up to 500 MB/s throughput at approximately 40% of the cost of gp3 at equivalent throughput. It's the correct choice when sequential throughput matters more than IOPS. io2 (A) is designed for IOPS-intensive OLTP workloads. gp3 (B) can deliver 1,000 MB/s but at higher cost than st1 for purely sequential workloads. sc1 (D) has lower throughput (250 MB/s maximum) and is for cold/archive data with infrequent access.
tags: Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload
Access options (for example, an S3 bucket with Requester Pays object storage)

stem: A company runs a database that requires 16,000 IOPS consistently. They currently use io1 and want to reduce costs. Which EBS volume type migration provides the same IOPS at lower cost?

answers.A: Migrate to gp2: gp2 provides up to 16,000 IOPS at 5,334 GB (3 IOPS/GB baseline).
answers.B: Migrate to gp3: configure 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s throughput independently — gp3 is approximately 20% cheaper than io1 at equivalent IOPS.
answers.C: Migrate to st1: st1 provides higher IOPS at lower cost.
answers.D: Migrate to sc1: cold HDD provides highest IOPS at lowest cost.

explanation: gp3 allows independent configuration of IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MB/s) regardless of volume size. gp3 is typically ~20% cheaper than io1 at equivalent IOPS for volumes needing 3,000-16,000 IOPS, making it the preferred migration target. gp2 (A) provides 16,000 IOPS but requires provisioning a 5,334 GB volume (3 IOPS/GB) which may exceed actual storage needs and cost more. st1 and sc1 (C, D) are HDD types with low IOPS, unsuitable for database workloads requiring consistent 16,000 IOPS.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)
Storage types with associated characteristics (for example, object, file, block)

stem: A company stores application logs in S3. Logs are frequently analyzed in the first 30 days, occasionally reviewed between 30-90 days, and rarely accessed after 90 days but must be retained for 7 years for compliance. Which S3 lifecycle policy minimizes cost?

answers.A: Store all logs in S3 Standard for 7 years.
answers.B: S3 Standard for 0-30 days → S3 Standard-IA for 30-90 days → S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for 90 days-1 year → S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year for the remaining 6 years.
answers.C: S3 Standard for 0-30 days → S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for 30 days → delete after 1 year.
answers.D: S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the full 7 years — it automatically optimizes costs.

explanation: A tiered lifecycle approach matches access patterns to storage costs: Standard for hot data (0-30d), Standard-IA for warm infrequent access (30-90d), Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely accessed (90d-1yr, instant retrieval when needed), and Glacier Deep Archive (lowest cost, $0.00099/GB/month) for the long compliance tail (1-7yr). All-Standard (A) wastes money. Option C deletes data after 1 year, violating the 7-year retention requirement. Intelligent-Tiering (D) works but incurs monitoring fees per object and doesn't reach Glacier Deep Archive prices.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: An S3 bucket receives millions of small objects (average 10 KB) per day. The company wants to use S3 lifecycle policies to move objects to S3 Glacier after 90 days. What cost consideration should they be aware of?

answers.A: S3 Glacier charges a minimum storage duration of 90 days — objects deleted before 90 days incur a pro-rated charge.
answers.B: Glacier has a minimum billable object size of 40 KB (32 KB metadata overhead + 8 KB user data overhead). For 10 KB objects, each will be billed as 40 KB, potentially costing more than S3 Standard for small objects.
answers.C: S3 lifecycle transitions are free, so small object size has no cost impact.
answers.D: S3 Glacier does not support objects smaller than 128 KB.

explanation: Glacier has a minimum billable object size: each archived object incurs 8 KB of user data overhead plus 32 KB of metadata storage, totaling 40 KB minimum billing regardless of actual object size. For 10 KB objects, you're billed for 40 KB — 4x the data. With millions of small objects, this overhead can make Glacier more expensive than Standard-IA or even Standard. The correct approach for small objects is to use S3 Batch Operations to consolidate them before archiving, or reconsider the archival strategy.
tags: Selecting the correct data lifecycle for storage
Determining the correct storage size for a workload

stem: A company's on-premises file servers access frequently updated shared project files. They want to extend storage to AWS S3 to reduce on-premises NAS costs while keeping low-latency access to hot files. Which AWS service is most appropriate?

answers.A: AWS DataSync: sync files from NAS to S3 on a schedule.
answers.B: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway: presents an NFS/SMB interface to on-premises clients, caches hot files locally, and stores all data in S3.
answers.C: AWS Transfer Family SFTP: provides an SFTP endpoint that writes directly to S3.
answers.D: Amazon EFS: mount as an NFS share from on-premises over Direct Connect.

explanation: Storage Gateway File Gateway is purpose-built for this use case: it presents standard file protocols (NFS/SMB) to on-premises clients with no application changes, caches frequently accessed files locally for low latency, and transparently stores all data in S3. This reduces on-premises NAS capacity requirements. DataSync (A) syncs files in batch but doesn't provide a low-latency cache or transparent file protocol interface. Transfer Family (C) is for managed SFTP endpoint access, not transparent file sharing. EFS (D) can be accessed over Direct Connect but is more expensive than S3 for cold data.
tags: AWS storage services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon FSx, Amazon EFS, Amazon S3, Amazon EBS)

stem: A company uses a tape library for backup. They want to modernize to AWS without changing their existing backup software. Which AWS service replaces the tape library?

answers.A: Amazon S3 Glacier: configure the backup software to use S3 Glacier as a target.
answers.B: AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway: presents a Virtual Tape Library (VTL) interface compatible with existing backup software (NetBackup, Veeam, etc.), and stores virtual tapes in S3 and Glacier.
answers.C: AWS Backup: create backup plans and vaults for all resources.
answers.D: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server: replace the tape library with a managed Windows file server.

explanation: Storage Gateway Tape Gateway emulates a physical tape library using the industry-standard iSCSI VTL interface. Existing backup software sees it as physical tapes and works without modification. Virtual tapes are stored in S3 and automatically archived to Glacier when 'ejected' to the virtual tape shelf. Configuring backup software to write directly to Glacier (A) requires software reconfiguration and Glacier doesn't present a VTL interface. AWS Backup (C) is a policy-based backup service, not a tape replacement. FSx (D) is file storage, not tape.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: An application uploads millions of small files (average 100 KB) to S3 individually. Upload throughput is limited to 50 MB/s. A developer proposes using S3 multipart upload. Would this help, and what is a better strategy?

answers.A: Multipart upload helps for files > 100 MB; for 100 KB files, batch multiple files into a single archive (e.g., .tar.gz) before uploading to reduce per-request overhead and improve throughput.
answers.B: Multipart upload always improves throughput regardless of file size.
answers.C: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for small files — it optimizes the TCP connection setup overhead.
answers.D: Use S3 Batch Operations to upload small files in parallel without code changes.

explanation: S3 multipart upload is recommended for objects > 100 MB — for 100 KB objects, the multipart API overhead outweighs any benefit. To improve throughput with small files, batch them into larger archives (tar, zip) before upload. This reduces the number of API calls (reducing per-request costs), allows multipart upload to be effective, and improves bandwidth utilization. Transfer Acceleration (C) reduces network latency on the path to S3, not per-request overhead for small files. S3 Batch Operations (D) operates on existing S3 objects, not uploads.
tags: Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload

stem: A company needs to upload a 100 GB file to S3 reliably. What is the correct approach and minimum recommended part size for S3 multipart upload?

answers.A: Upload the entire 100 GB as a single PUT request; S3 supports objects up to 5 TB in a single PUT.
answers.B: Use S3 multipart upload: split the file into parts of at least 5 MB (AWS minimum), upload parts in parallel for maximum throughput, then call CompleteMultipartUpload.
answers.C: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration with a single PUT request — it handles large files automatically.
answers.D: Split into parts of exactly 1 GB and upload sequentially to avoid part ordering issues.

explanation: S3 multipart upload is required for objects > 5 GB and strongly recommended for objects > 100 MB. Parts must be at least 5 MB (except the final part). Parts can be uploaded in parallel using multiple connections, significantly improving throughput and reliability (failed parts can be retried individually). Single PUT (A) is limited to 5 GB (not 5 TB). Transfer Acceleration (C) is a routing optimization, not a large-file upload mechanism. Sequential 1 GB parts (D) forgo the parallel throughput benefit.
tags: Determining the correct storage size for a workload

stem: A company provisions a 10 TB EBS io2 volume for a database but the database only uses 2 TB. io2 is billed per GB provisioned. What is the most cost-effective remediation?

answers.A: Enable EBS Auto Scaling to automatically reduce the volume size.
answers.B: Snapshot the existing volume, create a new 2 TB io2 volume (with the same IOPS configuration) from the snapshot, and attach it to the instance after detaching the old volume.
answers.C: Switch to an S3-backed instance store for the database to avoid EBS costs.
answers.D: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the EBS volume to move cold blocks to cheaper storage.

explanation: EBS volumes cannot be reduced in size (only increased). The correct approach is to snapshot the existing volume and create a smaller new volume from the snapshot, then swap it on the instance. This reduces EBS provisioned storage from 10 TB to 2 TB, cutting storage costs by 80%. EBS does not auto-scale down (A). Instance stores (C) are ephemeral and lose data on stop/terminate — not suitable for databases. EBS does not integrate with S3 Intelligent-Tiering (D) — that's an S3-specific feature.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company needs a shared file system for 20 Linux EC2 instances in the same AZ. The workload is random I/O and requires 3,000 IOPS consistently. They currently use EFS but find it too expensive for this use case. What is a more cost-effective alternative?

answers.A: Use a single EBS Multi-Attach io2 volume attached to all 20 instances simultaneously.
answers.B: Deploy Amazon FSx for Lustre in persistent mode with the required IOPS — FSx for Lustre provides higher performance at lower cost than EFS for IOPS-intensive workloads.
answers.C: Deploy an NFS server on EC2 backed by gp3 EBS volumes and share the NFS mount to all instances.
answers.D: Use EFS with Provisioned Throughput mode at the required level.

explanation: For small-scale shared NFS within a single AZ where full managed-service cost is not justified, a self-managed NFS server on EC2 with gp3 EBS volumes (3,000 IOPS baseline, no additional cost) is the most cost-effective approach. EBS Multi-Attach (A) supports up to 16 instances and requires cluster-aware filesystems — not standard for 20 instances. FSx for Lustre (B) is designed for HPC/ML workloads and isn't cheaper than EFS for general workloads at 3,000 IOPS. EFS Provisioned Throughput (D) charges additionally for provisioned throughput — same service, not cheaper.
tags: Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload

stem: A company stores user uploads on EBS gp3 volumes. Usage grows unpredictably and volumes are occasionally running out of space, causing application outages. Which is the most operationally simple solution?

answers.A: Provision EBS volumes at 10x the expected size to avoid running out.
answers.B: Migrate user uploads to Amazon S3, which automatically scales storage without capacity planning.
answers.C: Create a Lambda function that monitors EBS CloudWatch metrics and calls ModifyVolume to increase size when disk usage exceeds 80%.
answers.D: Enable EBS Auto Scaling in the EC2 console.

explanation: S3 automatically scales storage to any amount without provisioning or capacity planning — the exact problem with EBS. Migrating user uploads (objects) to S3 is the architecturally correct solution and eliminates storage capacity management entirely. Over-provisioning EBS (A) wastes money. Lambda + ModifyVolume (C) works but requires custom automation, testing, and the filesystem still needs to be extended inside the OS after the volume resize. There is no native 'EBS Auto Scaling' feature (D).

stem: An application uses an RDS database that is growing rapidly. The DBA is concerned about running out of storage during peak business hours. Which RDS feature addresses this?

answers.A: Enable Multi-AZ — the standby instance provides additional storage capacity.
answers.B: Enable RDS Storage Auto Scaling: set the maximum storage threshold; RDS automatically increases allocated storage when free space falls below 10% (or 10 GB/5 minutes), with no downtime.
answers.C: Schedule a nightly Lambda to call ModifyDBInstance and increase storage by 10%.
answers.D: Use Amazon Aurora, which automatically adjusts storage in 10 GB increments.

explanation: RDS Storage Auto Scaling monitors free storage space and automatically scales storage up to the configured maximum with no downtime. It triggers when free space < 10% of allocated storage, < 10 GB, and the condition lasts > 5 minutes. Multi-AZ (A) provides HA, not additional storage — both instances have the same storage allocation. Lambda scheduling (C) requires custom development and fixed-schedule increases. Aurora (D) does auto-scale in 10 GB increments, but the question asks about RDS, and Aurora is a separate engine with different pricing.

stem: A company uses S3 versioning for a bucket that stores CAD files. Versioning creates many old versions accumulating storage costs. They want to retain only the 5 most recent versions of each object. Which S3 feature achieves this?

answers.A: Create an S3 lifecycle rule to expire non-current versions older than 90 days.
answers.B: Create an S3 lifecycle rule with a NoncurrentVersionExpiration action that expires non-current versions after retaining the newest N versions — set NoncurrentVersions to 5.
answers.C: Disable versioning to stop creating new versions; delete old versions manually.
answers.D: Use S3 Object Lock retention policies to limit versions to 5 per object.

explanation: S3 lifecycle rules support NoncurrentVersionExpiration with a NoncurrentVersions count parameter that retains only the N newest non-current versions and expires older ones automatically. This is the purpose-built mechanism for limiting version accumulation. Expiring by age (A) doesn't guarantee keeping exactly 5 versions — a burst of changes could lose more versions than intended. Disabling versioning (C) stops new versions but doesn't delete old ones, and loses the protection versioning provides. Object Lock (D) is for WORM compliance retention, not version count limiting.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company needs to back up RDS databases, EBS volumes, DynamoDB tables, and EFS file systems using a single policy-driven service with cross-region and cross-account backup support. Which service meets all these requirements?

answers.A: Use native service backups: RDS automated backups, EBS snapshots, DynamoDB point-in-time recovery, and EFS backup.
answers.B: AWS Backup: centralized backup service with policies (backup plans), supports all listed services, and provides cross-region and cross-account copy capabilities from a single console.
answers.C: AWS DataSync: sync all data to another region for backup purposes.
answers.D: Amazon S3 with Lambda: store all backups in S3 and use Lambda to orchestrate cross-region copies.

explanation: AWS Backup is the purpose-built centralized backup management service that supports RDS, EBS, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, EC2, FSx, and more. It provides backup plans with retention policies, cross-region copy rules, cross-account sharing, and compliance reporting — all from one console. Native service backups (A) work but require managing each service's backup mechanism independently without a unified policy. DataSync (C) syncs data but isn't a backup solution with point-in-time recovery. Custom S3+Lambda (D) requires significant development and maintenance.
tags: AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

stem: A company must retain financial records for 7 years and ensure they cannot be deleted or modified by anyone, including AWS account administrators. Which S3 configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Enable S3 Versioning and restrict delete permissions with IAM policies.
answers.B: Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period: no user, including the root account, can delete or overwrite locked objects during the retention period.
answers.C: Enable S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period.
answers.D: Store objects in S3 Glacier with a Vault Lock policy defining a 7-year retention.

explanation: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode creates immutable storage that cannot be overridden by any user — including the root account and AWS Support. Objects cannot be deleted or overwritten for the retention period. This satisfies SEC Rule 17a-4(f) and similar financial compliance requirements. Governance mode (C) allows users with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission to override the lock — not suitable for strict compliance. Versioning with IAM (A) can be circumvented by privileged users. Glacier Vault Lock (D) is valid but the question asks about S3, and Vault Lock is for Glacier specifically.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company needs to migrate 100 TB of data from an on-premises NFS share to Amazon EFS. The migration must run continuously while the production NFS server remains live, with minimal impact on production workloads. Which service is most appropriate?

answers.A: AWS Snowball: ship data physically from the NFS server to AWS.
answers.B: AWS DataSync: configure a DataSync agent on-premises to read from NFS, transfer data to EFS over Direct Connect or VPN with bandwidth throttling, and incrementally sync changes.
answers.C: Use rsync over Direct Connect: manually configure rsync with compression and bandwidth limiting.
answers.D: AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway: use as a migration path from on-premises NFS to EFS.

explanation: AWS DataSync is purpose-built for live NFS-to-EFS migration. The on-premises DataSync agent reads from the NFS source, transfers data using optimized multipart transfers (10x faster than rsync), verifies integrity, and supports incremental syncs to catch changes since the last transfer. It supports bandwidth throttling to avoid impacting production workloads. Snowball (A) is for offline bulk transfers — not live migrations with ongoing changes. rsync (C) works but is slower, requires manual configuration, and lacks built-in integrity verification. Storage Gateway (D) is for ongoing hybrid access, not a migration tool.
tags: Selecting the appropriate service for data migration to storage services

stem: A media company migrates 500 TB of video assets from on-premises object storage (Swift) to Amazon S3. The existing system uses an HTTP API. Which approach requires the least custom development?

answers.A: Write a Python script using boto3 and the Swift SDK to stream objects from Swift and upload to S3.
answers.B: Use AWS DataSync with a custom agent plugin for Swift-compatible object storage.
answers.C: Use S3 Batch Operations to copy objects in bulk from the Swift endpoint.
answers.D: Contact AWS Professional Services to build a custom migration pipeline.

explanation: For HTTP-based object storage (Swift), a Python script using the Swift SDK to download objects and boto3 to upload to S3 with multipart upload is the most practical approach. DataSync (B) supports NFS, SMB, S3, EFS, FSx, and HDFS — it does not have a native Swift connector. S3 Batch Operations (C) operates on existing S3 objects, not external systems. AWS Professional Services (D) is an option but not 'least custom development' — a simple Python script achieves the same result.

stem: A company stores machine learning training datasets in S3. Datasets are accessed multiple times per day during model training sprints (lasting 2-3 weeks) then not accessed for months until the next training sprint. Which storage strategy is most cost-effective?

answers.A: S3 Standard at all times — training access patterns are frequent during sprints.
answers.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: automatically moves objects to lower-cost tiers during the inactive period and back to frequent-access tier when training resumes, with no retrieval fees.
answers.C: S3 Standard-IA: lower cost, but retrieval fees apply during intensive training sprints.
answers.D: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: lowest cost, retrieval in milliseconds for training access.

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with unknown or changing access patterns. It automatically moves objects between Frequent Access, Infrequent Access, and Archive tiers based on activity with no retrieval fees when data moves back to Frequent Access. During training sprints, objects stay in Frequent Access tier (same cost as Standard). During dormant periods, they move to cheaper tiers automatically. Standard (A) is correct during sprints but wastes money during dormancy. Standard-IA (C) charges retrieval fees which are expensive during intensive daily training. Glacier Instant Retrieval (D) has higher retrieval costs than Standard at the volume of ML training reads.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company needs to store compliance audit logs for exactly 1 year, after which they must be permanently deleted. The logs are never accessed after creation except during rare compliance audits. Which S3 configuration meets this requirement at lowest cost?

answers.A: Store in S3 Standard with a lifecycle rule to delete after 365 days.
answers.B: Store in S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Object Lock governance mode and a lifecycle expiration rule at 365 days.
answers.C: Store in S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a lifecycle expiration rule at 365 days — at $0.00099/GB/month this is the lowest cost storage for rarely accessed data.
answers.D: Store in S3 One Zone-IA with a lifecycle rule to delete after 365 days.

explanation: Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage at $0.00099/GB/month — appropriate for data rarely accessed but requiring long-term retention. A lifecycle expiration rule at 365 days auto-deletes objects. Retrieval is measured in hours, acceptable for rare compliance audits. S3 Standard (A) costs ~12x more. Object Lock governance mode (B) prevents deletion during the retention period — contradicting the requirement to delete at 365 days with Object Lock in place. One Zone-IA (D) stores data in a single AZ and risks data loss from AZ failure; compliance logs usually require multi-AZ durability.
tags: Selecting the correct data lifecycle for storage

stem: A company uses S3 with versioning enabled. Old object versions accumulate significantly over time. They want to automatically move non-current versions to Glacier after 30 days and delete them after 1 year. Which S3 lifecycle configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Enable S3 Object Lock with a 1-year governance period on all objects.
answers.B: Create a lifecycle rule with two actions: NoncurrentVersionTransition to Glacier after 30 days, and NoncurrentVersionExpiration after 365 days.
answers.C: Create a lifecycle rule with CurrentVersionExpiration after 365 days.
answers.D: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket — it handles versioned objects automatically.

explanation: Versioned S3 lifecycle rules have specific actions for non-current versions: NoncurrentVersionTransition moves old versions to cheaper storage classes after N days, and NoncurrentVersionExpiration permanently deletes them after N days. Both actions apply only to non-current (previous) versions, leaving the current version unaffected. Object Lock (A) prevents deletion — opposite of the intent. CurrentVersionExpiration (C) applies to current versions, not non-current. Intelligent-Tiering (D) doesn't manage version lifecycle — it only moves the current version between tiers.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company's S3 lifecycle policy transitions objects to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days. An analyst needs to access a Glaciered object immediately. They restore it with Expedited retrieval and begin analysis. The analyst then tries to delete the object from Glacier before the 90-day minimum storage duration is reached. What is the cost implication?

answers.A: The object is deleted immediately with no additional cost.
answers.B: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval has a 90-day minimum storage duration. Deleting before 90 days incurs a pro-rated charge for the remaining days of the minimum period.
answers.C: Expedited retrieval automatically moves the object back to S3 Standard, avoiding Glacier deletion fees.
answers.D: Glacier objects cannot be deleted; they can only expire based on lifecycle policy.

explanation: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval has a 90-day minimum storage duration. If an object is deleted (or transitioned out) before 90 days, you are charged for the remaining days at the Glacier storage rate. This is a common cost trap with Glacier. Expedited retrieval (C) creates a temporary copy accessible for access but doesn't change the storage class or avoid the minimum duration charge. Objects can be deleted (D) but incur the minimum storage fee.
tags: Access options (for example, an S3 bucket with Requester Pays object storage)

stem: A company is choosing storage for three workloads: (1) a web application serving static assets to users globally, (2) a database requiring block storage with 3,000 IOPS, and (3) a machine learning team sharing 100 TB of training data across 50 EC2 instances. Which storage service mapping is correct and most cost-effective?

answers.A: S3 for all three workloads — it's the cheapest AWS storage.
answers.B: (1) S3 + CloudFront for static assets; (2) EBS gp3 for the database; (3) EFS for shared ML training data across instances.
answers.C: (1) EFS for static assets; (2) Instance store for the database; (3) S3 for ML training data.
answers.D: (1) S3; (2) EBS io2 for maximum IOPS; (3) S3 with each instance mounting separately.

explanation: (1) S3+CloudFront: S3 is the canonical object store for static assets; CloudFront caches globally for performance. (2) EBS gp3: provides 3,000 IOPS baseline with no additional cost, purpose-built for block storage workloads like databases. (3) EFS: managed NFS file system that scales to petabytes and supports concurrent access from all 50 instances simultaneously. S3 for all (A) doesn't provide block storage for databases. Instance store (C-2) is ephemeral. Multiple S3 mounts (D-3) requires custom tooling (s3fs) and is not suitable for shared POSIX file access by ML frameworks.

stem: A company stores 1 PB of data in S3. 10% is accessed daily, 30% is accessed monthly, and 60% has not been accessed in over a year. They want to optimize cost without changing application code. Which S3 feature automatically optimizes storage costs based on access patterns?

answers.A: S3 Cross-Region Replication: replicate cold data to a lower-cost region.
answers.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering: monitors access patterns per object and automatically moves each object between Frequent Access, Infrequent Access, Archive Instant Access, and Archive tiers with no retrieval fees.
answers.C: S3 Lifecycle policies: create rules for each percentage of data.
answers.D: S3 Storage Class Analysis: analyzes access patterns and generates lifecycle recommendations.

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each object to the most cost-effective tier based on access frequency: Frequent Access (same cost as Standard) for hot data, Infrequent Access for data not accessed for 30 days, Archive Instant Access for 90+ days, and Archive for 180+ days. There are no retrieval fees for transitioning back to Frequent Access. For 1 PB of mixed access patterns, Intelligent-Tiering optimizes automatically per object. Lifecycle policies (C) apply fixed rules regardless of actual access patterns. Storage Class Analysis (D) only recommends — it doesn't act.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company stores application logs in S3 Standard. AWS Cost Explorer shows that 90% of storage costs come from logs older than 90 days that are never accessed. What is the most cost-effective remediation?

answers.A: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket for automatic optimization.
answers.B: Create an S3 lifecycle rule to transition objects older than 90 days to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and expire them after 7 years, reducing storage cost by up to 95%.
answers.C: Enable S3 Requester Pays to shift log access costs to the team reading the logs.
answers.D: Compress logs before storing in S3 Standard to reduce storage volume.

explanation: If logs older than 90 days are never accessed, moving them to Glacier Deep Archive ($0.00099/GB/month vs $0.023/GB/month for Standard) reduces costs by ~96%. A lifecycle transition rule is the simplest implementation. Intelligent-Tiering (A) has a monitoring fee per object and wouldn't reach Deep Archive prices for data that is never accessed. Requester Pays (C) shifts cost of access, not storage cost. Compression (D) reduces storage volume but not the per-GB price — and doesn't address the fundamental issue of paying Standard prices for cold data.
tags: Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

stem: A company evaluates three storage types for different workloads. Match the correct storage type (object, file, block) to each workload and identify the lowest-cost AWS service for each: (1) hosting 10 million static images for a web application, (2) sharing configuration files across 10 Linux EC2 instances, (3) storing a MySQL database requiring low-latency random IOPS.

answers.B: (1) S3 (object, lowest cost at $0.023/GB), (2) EFS (file, NFS-compatible shared access), (3) EBS gp3 (block, random IOPS for database)
answers.D: (1) S3, (2) EBS with NFS server, (3) S3 with POSIX adapter

explanation: S3 (object storage) at $0.023/GB is the lowest-cost option for static images — it's designed for web-scale object hosting with direct HTTP access. EFS (file storage) provides NFS-compatible shared access across multiple instances with no capacity planning. EBS gp3 (block storage) provides the low-latency random IOPS required by relational databases, with data accessible only to one instance at a time. EFS for images (A-1) costs more than S3. EBS with an NFS server (D-2) works but requires managing an EC2 instance. S3 with POSIX adapter (D-3) is complex and not suitable for production databases.

stem: A company wants to reduce EC2 costs for production workloads that run 24/7 for at least 3 years. Which purchasing option provides the maximum discount?

answers.A: Spot Instances with Spot Fleet to handle interruptions.
answers.B: 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the specific instance type and region, providing up to 72% discount compared to On-Demand.
answers.C: 3-year Compute Savings Plans: same 3-year commitment but provides discount flexibility across instance families and regions.
answers.D: On-Demand Instances with auto-scaling to minimize idle capacity.

explanation: 3-year All Upfront Standard Reserved Instances provide the maximum EC2 discount (up to 72%). They apply to a specific instance type, OS, tenancy, and region. Compute Savings Plans (C) provide up to 66% discount with more flexibility (any instance family, region, OS, tenancy). For stable, known workloads where flexibility is not needed, Standard RIs provide the highest savings. Spot (A) provides 70-90% discount but with interruption risk — unsuitable for production 24/7 workloads. On-Demand with auto-scaling (D) has no committed discount.
