stem: A startup is building a React single-page application (SPA) with CI/CD from a GitHub repository. They need preview environments for every pull request, custom domain support with HTTPS, and backend environment variable injection at build time. They want to minimize operational overhead. Which setup is most appropriate?

answers.A: Set up an S3 bucket with static website hosting and CloudFront distribution. Write a GitHub Actions workflow to sync build output to S3 and invalidate the CloudFront cache on every push. Manually provision certificates via ACM.
answers.B: Use AWS Amplify Hosting connected to the GitHub repository. Configure branch-based deployments with PR preview environments enabled. Add environment variables in the Amplify Console. Amplify automatically provisions CloudFront, S3, HTTPS certificates, and per-PR preview URLs.
answers.C: Deploy the SPA on AWS Elastic Beanstalk with a Node.js platform. Configure CodePipeline to trigger on GitHub push events. Use Elastic Beanstalk environments for production and staging.
answers.D: Use AWS CodeCommit to mirror the GitHub repo, CodeBuild to compile the React app, and CodeDeploy to push output to S3. Use CloudFront with ACM for HTTPS.

explanation: Amplify Hosting natively supports GitHub CI/CD integration, automatic PR preview environments (each PR gets a unique URL), custom domains with automatic ACM certificate provisioning, and build-time environment variable injection—all with zero infrastructure management. The S3+CloudFront approach (A) requires manual CI/CD, certificate provisioning, and lacks built-in PR preview support. Elastic Beanstalk (C) is server-based, inappropriate for static SPAs. CodeCommit mirroring (D) adds unnecessary steps since Amplify integrates natively with GitHub.
tags: Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)
How to appropriately use edge accelerators (for example, content delivery network [CDN])

stem: An Amplify application uses Amplify Auth (backed by Amazon Cognito) for user authentication. The company wants to allow users to sign in with their existing Google Workspace corporate accounts via OIDC federation. After sign-in, authenticated users must access a private S3 bucket to retrieve their personal documents (stored at s3://bucket/user-id/). The S3 access must be scoped to each user's own prefix only. How should the architect configure this?

answers.A: Configure Google as a Social Identity Provider in Cognito User Pool. After federation, issue each user a pre-signed S3 URL from a Lambda function (triggered post-authentication) scoped to their prefix.
answers.B: Use Cognito User Pool with Google OIDC federation. Grant the Cognito Identity Pool authenticated role full S3 access. In the application, prefix all S3 API calls with the user's sub claim to restrict access in application code.
answers.C: Configure Google Workspace as an OIDC provider in the Cognito User Pool. Set up a Cognito Identity Pool linked to the User Pool. Configure the authenticated IAM role with an S3 policy using the cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub condition variable to scope access to s3://bucket/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/* only.
answers.D: Use the Amplify DataStore to abstract all S3 access behind a GraphQL API. The AppSync API enforces per-user authorization using Cognito claims. Users never access S3 directly.

explanation: Cognito Identity Pools generate temporary AWS credentials for authenticated users. The IAM role policy can use the cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub condition variable, which resolves to the user's unique Cognito identity ID, enabling fine-grained S3 prefix-level authorization enforced by IAM—not application code. This is the AWS-recommended pattern. Pre-signed URLs from Lambda (A) add a server-side component and don't enforce IAM-level least privilege. Full S3 access enforced only in app code (B) relies on application-level controls that can be bypassed. DataStore/AppSync (D) changes the architecture fundamentally and adds unnecessary complexity.
tags: Design secure access to AWS resources
AWS federated access and identity services (for example, IAM, AWS IAM Identity Center)
Security services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cognito, AWS GuardDuty, AWS Macie)
Designing a role-based access control strategy (for example, AWS STS, role switching, cross-account access)

stem: A mobile app team needs to run automated UI tests (Appium Python) on their iOS and Android app before each release. They must test on 50 specific real device models (including older iOS/Android versions) to verify compatibility. Tests currently take 8 hours sequentially on the team's physical device lab. They want to reduce test execution to under 30 minutes. Which AWS Device Farm configuration achieves this?

answers.A: Upload the test package and app to AWS Device Farm. Create a test run with a custom device pool containing the 50 required real device models. Device Farm runs the Appium tests in parallel across all 50 devices simultaneously, reducing total test time to the duration of the longest single test suite (typically 15-25 minutes).
answers.B: Use Device Farm's simulated device feature to emulate all 50 device models simultaneously. Simulations run faster than real devices and can scale to hundreds of instances.
answers.C: Configure Device Farm with 50 concurrent EC2 instances running Android emulators and iOS simulators via XCUITest. Use Step Functions to orchestrate parallel test execution.
answers.D: Use AWS CodeBuild with parallelism configured to 50 concurrent builds, each running an Appium test against a Device Farm simulated device via the Device Farm API.

explanation: AWS Device Farm runs tests on real physical devices (not simulations) in parallel. A custom device pool with 50 selected models executes all tests concurrently, reducing time from 8 hours to roughly the length of one test run (~15-25 minutes). Device Farm doesn't use simulated devices for real-device testing (B is incorrect—Device Farm has real devices, not emulation-based simulations for this use case). EC2 emulators (C) can't run real iOS testing. CodeBuild + Device Farm API (D) adds complexity and misunderstands Device Farm's parallel execution model.
tags: Design high-performing and elastic compute solutions
Scalability capabilities with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, AWS Auto Scaling)

stem: A banking app team uses AWS Device Farm for mobile testing. Their app connects to internal backend services that are not publicly accessible (running in a private VPC). The app on the Device Farm real devices cannot reach the internal APIs, causing all integration tests to fail. How should the architect enable Device Farm to access the private backend?

answers.A: Create a VPN connection from the Device Farm testing network to the corporate network. Device Farm automatically connects to VPNs configured in the test specification.
answers.B: Expose the internal backend via an internet-facing ALB with IP whitelisting to AWS Device Farm's published IP ranges.
answers.C: Use AWS Device Farm's Private Device feature with a private device slot. Configure a Device Farm VPC connection that creates a PrivateLink or VPC peering connection to the VPC hosting the internal backend. Tests run on privately managed devices that can reach the internal VPC.
answers.D: Use Device Farm's built-in network shaping feature to configure a custom DNS entry pointing the app's backend hostname to the internal VPC's private IP address.

explanation: AWS Device Farm Private Devices allow enterprises to connect device slots to their own VPC using VPC peering or PrivateLink. This gives the real device network access to private backend services without exposing them to the internet. Standard (public) Device Farm devices are in a shared AWS network with no access to private VPCs. VPN in test specs (A) isn't a native Device Farm capability. IP whitelisting public Device Farm IPs (B) exposes the backend. Network shaping (D) is for simulating network conditions, not routing to private IPs.
tags: Network connection options (for example, AWS VPN, AWS Direct Connect, AWS PrivateLink)

stem: A law firm wants to build an intelligent search system using Amazon Kendra over their document corpus: 200,000 documents in SharePoint Online, 50,000 in S3, and 10,000 in a custom internal database. Users must only see search results for documents they are authorized to view (same ACLs as SharePoint). The solution must update the index within 1 hour of document changes. Which architecture meets these requirements?

answers.A: Use the Kendra SharePoint connector and S3 connector. For the custom database, write a custom data source connector using Lambda. Set all connectors to run full crawls every hour. Disable user context filtering; enforce authorization in the application layer.
answers.B: Configure the Kendra SharePoint Online connector (native) with user context (token-based ACL filtering) to sync SharePoint ACLs. Configure the S3 connector with metadata files defining ACLs per document. Implement a custom data source connector for the internal database using the Kendra Custom Data Source API. Schedule incremental syncs every 30-60 minutes. Enable user context filtering at query time using the user's token.
answers.C: Index all documents in OpenSearch Service. Write a Lambda function to extract ACLs from SharePoint and store in DynamoDB. At query time, filter OpenSearch results against DynamoDB ACLs. Use Kendra to re-rank OpenSearch results for relevance.
answers.D: Use Kendra with the SharePoint and S3 connectors. For ACL enforcement, configure a post-query Lambda function that calls the SharePoint Graph API to verify each search result against the user's permissions before returning results.

explanation: Kendra natively supports user context filtering using ACLs ingested from SharePoint (via the native connector which imports SharePoint ACLs) and from S3 metadata. A Custom Data Source connector handles the internal database. Incremental syncs every 30-60 minutes meet the 1-hour freshness requirement. Kendra applies ACL filtering at query time using the user's token/email, ensuring users see only authorized results. Disabling ACL filtering (A) violates the requirement. OpenSearch with Lambda ACL checks (C) loses Kendra's semantic search and is complex. Post-query Lambda ACL verification (D) is slow, doesn't scale, and may still return unauthorized document titles in result snippets.
tags: AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)

stem: A pharmaceutical company deploys Amazon Kendra to search internal research documents. Scientists complain that searches for 'myocardial infarction' don't return documents that use only 'heart attack' or 'MI', and vice versa. Additionally, documents from the last 6 months should rank higher than older documents. Relevance tuning has not been configured. Which Kendra features should the solutions architect configure?

answers.A: Enable Amazon Comprehend Medical as a post-processing step to normalize medical terminology in search queries before passing to Kendra. Implement a Lambda function to reweight results by date.
answers.B: Use Kendra's thesaurus feature (custom synonym file) to define bidirectional synonyms between 'myocardial infarction', 'heart attack', and 'MI'. Configure field relevance tuning by boosting the document 'created_date' field with a DURATION freshness boost in the Kendra index configuration.
answers.C: Edit all documents to include all synonym variants in each document's metadata. Reindex the corpus. Use custom attributes for date ranking.
answers.D: Upload a custom thesaurus file to the Kendra index defining synonyms for the medical terms. In the Kendra index field mappings, map the document date field to a DATE type attribute. Enable freshness tuning on that attribute with a freshness duration that boosts documents created within 6 months.

explanation: Kendra supports custom thesauri (synonym files in plain text format) that expand queries to include synonyms at search time—no document reindexing needed. Freshness tuning is a native Kendra relevance feature that boosts documents based on a DATE field, configurable per-index. Together these address both requirements without custom code. Amazon Comprehend Medical (A) adds complexity and isn't a supported Kendra integration point. Editing all documents (C) is operationally expensive and brittle. Option D is the correct specific implementation; B describes the same approach but is less precisely stated regarding the freshness boost configuration.
tags: AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)
Data access patterns (for example, read-intensive compared with write-intensive)

stem: A data science team trains large deep learning models on SageMaker using ml.p3.16xlarge instances. Training jobs run for 12-18 hours. They want to use Spot Instances to reduce cost by up to 70% but are concerned about interruptions losing training progress. The training framework (PyTorch) supports checkpoint saves to disk. Which SageMaker configuration handles interruptions correctly?

answers.A: Enable Managed Spot Training in the SageMaker training job. Set MaxWaitTimeInSeconds to 86400. The job will automatically retry from the beginning if interrupted. Spot interruptions rarely occur for GPU instances.
answers.B: Use SageMaker Managed Spot Training with a checkpoint S3 URI. The SageMaker SDK automatically saves checkpoints at fixed intervals. Configure the PyTorch training script to load from S3 on startup.
answers.C: Enable Managed Spot Training in the SageMaker Estimator with a checkpoint_s3_uri and checkpoint_local_path. Modify the PyTorch training script to periodically save checkpoints to checkpoint_local_path; SageMaker automatically syncs these to the S3 URI. On restart after interruption, SageMaker copies the latest checkpoint from S3 to checkpoint_local_path before resuming training.
answers.D: Use SageMaker Warm Pools to retain ml.p3.16xlarge instances between training runs. This eliminates interruption risk while reducing provisioning overhead.

explanation: SageMaker Managed Spot Training requires the training script to implement checkpointing to a local path (checkpoint_local_path). SageMaker syncs this path to the specified S3 URI during training and restores from it on restart. The SDK does not automatically checkpoint—the script must. MaxWaitTimeInSeconds controls how long to wait for spot capacity. Restarting from the beginning (A) defeats the purpose of checkpointing. SageMaker Warm Pools (D) keep compute warm between jobs but don't protect against spot interruptions during a job.
tags: AWS purchasing options (for example, Spot Instances, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans)

stem: A company has 1,500 customer-specific ML models (each 50 MB, XGBoost). Each customer calls their dedicated model infrequently (average 2 requests/day). The company also has a 3-stage inference pipeline where request data must flow through a preprocessing Lambda, an XGBoost scoring model, and a post-processing model sequentially for each request. Cost optimization is a priority. Which SageMaker endpoint type should be used for each use case?

answers.A: Use a SageMaker Multi-Model Endpoint (MME) for the 1,500 customer models—MME dynamically loads and caches models from S3, sharing compute across all models and dramatically reducing cost. Use a SageMaker Inference Pipeline (multi-container endpoint) for the 3-stage sequential pipeline, chaining preprocessing, XGBoost, and post-processing containers.
answers.B: Deploy each of the 1,500 models as individual SageMaker endpoints. Use Step Functions to orchestrate the 3-stage inference pipeline, calling each stage as a separate SageMaker endpoint.
answers.C: Use a Multi-Model Endpoint for the 3-stage pipeline by packaging all three models as a single MME. Use individual endpoints for each of the 1,500 models to guarantee isolation.
answers.D: Use SageMaker Serverless Inference for the 1,500 customer models (pay per invocation, scales to zero). Use Batch Transform for the 3-stage pipeline to process all customer requests nightly.

explanation: Multi-Model Endpoints are purpose-built for hosting thousands of models on shared compute, loading/unloading from S3 based on traffic—ideal for 1,500 infrequently-called models. Inference Pipelines chain up to 15 containers on a single endpoint for sequential real-time inference—exactly the 3-stage requirement. Individual endpoints (B) for 1,500 models would cost enormously. MME doesn't support multi-stage pipelines (C). Serverless Inference (D) could work for the customer models but Batch Transform isn't suitable for synchronous pipeline inference.
tags: Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)
Optimization of compute utilization (for example, containers, serverless computing, microservices)
Determining cost-effective AWS compute services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate)

stem: A mortgage company needs to extract structured data from 500-page loan application packages stored in S3 as multi-page PDFs. Each package contains forms (with key-value pairs) and tables (amortization schedules). Processing must be asynchronous, and extracted data must be validated and stored in DynamoDB within 10 minutes of upload. The solution must be fully serverless. Which architecture is correct?

answers.A: Use Amazon Textract's synchronous AnalyzeDocument API from a Lambda function. Process each PDF page in a separate Lambda invocation. Store results in DynamoDB. Lambda's 15-minute timeout handles large documents.
answers.B: An S3 event triggers a Lambda function that calls Textract StartDocumentAnalysis (async) with FORMS and TABLES feature types, specifying an SNS notification topic. When analysis completes, SNS triggers a second Lambda that calls GetDocumentAnalysis to retrieve paginated results, parses forms and tables from the Textract response blocks, validates data, and writes to DynamoDB.
answers.C: Use Amazon Comprehend to extract entities from the PDFs directly. Store entity data in DynamoDB. Use Textract only for OCR on scanned documents.
answers.D: Use AWS Glue to process the PDFs with a custom Python script (boto3 Textract calls) in a Spark job. Store results in DynamoDB using the DynamoDB connector.

explanation: Textract's synchronous API has page limits (single-page images or up to 3,000 pages via async) and cannot handle 500-page PDFs synchronously within Lambda's execution limits. StartDocumentAnalysis (async) processes multi-page PDFs end-to-end; SNS notification triggers result retrieval, enabling fully serverless event-driven processing. Comprehend (C) extracts NLP entities, not structured form/table data. Glue Spark jobs (D) add operational complexity and aren't truly serverless in this context.
tags: Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
Serverless technologies and patterns (for example, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda)
Determine high-performing data ingestion and transformation solutions

stem: A healthcare company processes insurance claim forms using Amazon Textract. The forms vary in layout across 20 insurance providers, making key-value pair extraction unreliable (the same field appears in different positions and with different labels across forms). The team needs to reliably extract 10 specific fields (patient name, date of birth, diagnosis code, claim amount, etc.) regardless of form layout. Which Textract capability should they use?

answers.A: Use AnalyzeDocument with FORMS feature type and post-process key-value pairs using fuzzy matching on key names to identify the 10 target fields.
answers.B: Use AnalyzeDocument with LAYOUT feature type to identify document structure, then write custom parsing logic to locate each field based on spatial coordinates.
answers.C: Use AnalyzeDocument with the QUERIES feature type. Define 10 natural language queries (e.g., 'What is the patient name?', 'What is the diagnosis code?'). Textract uses ML to locate and extract the answer regardless of its position or label in the document.
answers.D: Train a custom Amazon Rekognition model to identify and extract the 10 specific fields from the claim form images based on their expected positions in a reference layout.

explanation: Amazon Textract Queries allow users to ask specific natural language questions about a document, and Textract's ML model finds the answer regardless of where it appears or how the label is worded. This is specifically designed for layout-variable documents where FORMS-based key-value extraction fails due to label inconsistency. Fuzzy matching on FORMS output (A) is fragile and requires maintenance. LAYOUT-based spatial parsing (B) requires complex custom logic. Rekognition (D) is for image recognition, not structured document extraction.
tags: AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)
Data transformation services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Glue)

stem: A pharmaceutical company transcribes recorded calls between medical representatives and physicians. Transcription accuracy is poor for drug brand names (e.g., 'Ozempic', 'Keytruda') and clinical terms (e.g., 'subcutaneous', 'contraindication'). The company has a corpus of 500 hours of existing transcribed call recordings. Which Transcribe feature provides the greatest accuracy improvement?

answers.A: Enable the Amazon Transcribe Medical specialty model, which is trained on clinical and pharmaceutical terminology.
answers.B: Add a Custom Vocabulary list with all drug names and clinical terms. Custom Vocabulary teaches Transcribe how to spell and weight specific words.
answers.C: Train a Custom Language Model (CLM) using the existing 500 hours of transcribed call recordings as training data. CLMs adapt the base acoustic and language models to domain-specific vocabulary, context, and speaking patterns, providing the highest accuracy improvement for specialized domains.
answers.D: Use the Transcribe batch transcription API with the en-US-Medical model and post-process with a custom medical entity normalizer using Amazon Comprehend Medical.

explanation: Custom Language Models (CLMs) train Transcribe on domain-specific text corpora, adapting the language model to pharmaceutical terminology, brand names, and clinical context. With 500 hours of transcribed data, a CLM provides substantially better accuracy than a Custom Vocabulary list alone, which only adds pronunciation and spelling hints for specific words. Transcribe Medical (A) is designed for physician-dictated clinical notes, not sales call conversations, and the model isn't fine-tuned to brand-specific drug names. Post-processing with Comprehend Medical (D) corrects entity extraction but not transcription accuracy.
tags: AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)
Determine high-performing data ingestion and transformation solutions

stem: A financial services company records customer service calls for quality assurance. Each call has an agent and a customer speaking. The company needs transcription that (1) labels each speaker separately, (2) redacts PII (account numbers, SSNs, dates of birth) from the transcript stored in S3, and (3) generates a separate audio file with PII portions silenced for compliance playback. Which Transcribe configuration achieves all three requirements?

answers.A: Enable speaker diarization (ShowSpeakerLabels: true, MaxSpeakerLabels: 2) in the transcription job settings. Enable PII identification and redaction (ContentRedaction: redactedAndUnredacted) targeting account numbers, SSN, and date of birth. Transcribe outputs a redacted transcript and a redacted audio file to S3. Store the redacted versions for compliance; use the unredacted transcript only for internal authorized analysis.
answers.B: Transcribe the call without diarization. Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities post-transcription. Build a Lambda function to redact PII from the transcript. Use Amazon Polly to regenerate the audio with PII sections replaced by silence.
answers.C: Enable diarization and channel identification simultaneously. Transcribe each channel as a separate audio track and merge transcripts. Use a Lambda function to detect and redact PII using regex patterns.
answers.D: Use Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics, which provides speaker diarization, sentiment analysis, and PII redaction in a single API call optimized for contact center use cases.

explanation: Transcribe natively supports speaker diarization and PII content redaction in a single job. The ContentRedaction setting with redactedAndUnredacted mode outputs both a redacted transcript and a redacted audio file (with PII segments silenced) to S3. This meets all three requirements without custom Lambda code. Amazon Comprehend + Lambda (B) doesn't produce a redacted audio file natively. Channel identification + diarization (C) are mutually exclusive settings in Transcribe. Option D (Transcribe Call Analytics) is also technically correct and even more appropriate for contact center calls—it provides diarization, PII redaction, and sentiment—making D a valid answer, but A also correctly describes the native Transcribe capabilities for this scenario.
tags: Implementing policies for data access, lifecycle, and protection
AWS Managed Services (AMS) with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon Comprehend, Amazon Polly)

stem: A global e-commerce company uses Amazon Translate to localize product descriptions in 15 languages. Brand names and proprietary product terms (e.g., 'HyperGlide Technology', 'ClearView Pro') must never be translated—they must appear verbatim in all target languages. Additionally, certain existing human-translated phrases (full sentences used in marketing) must be used exactly as-is instead of machine translation. Which Translate features address both requirements?

answers.A: Use Active Custom Translation for brand names by providing a parallel corpus of brand name examples. Use the do-not-translate XML tag in source text to preserve marketing phrases.
answers.B: Use Custom Terminology (CT) to define brand names and product terms that must appear verbatim in output. Use Parallel Data with Active Custom Translation (ACT) to provide existing human-translated sentence pairs that override machine translation for those specific segments.
answers.C: Use Custom Terminology for both requirements: add brand names as single-term entries and add full marketing sentences as multi-word terminology entries.
answers.D: Pre-process the source text to replace brand names with placeholders (e.g., [TERM_1]). Translate the modified text. Post-process to replace placeholders with the original terms.

explanation: Custom Terminology (CT) is designed for verbatim term substitution (brand names, product terms) and guarantees those terms appear unchanged in translated output. Active Custom Translation (ACT) with Parallel Data provides human-translated sentence pairs that override MT for full segments—exactly for the marketing phrase requirement. Multi-word terminology entries in CT (C) don't reliably match full sentences in varied contexts. Placeholder preprocessing (D) is a workaround that can corrupt sentence structure and doesn't handle full-sentence phrase overrides.
